Within the data center and cloud hosting environment, administrators must check out privileged credentials from the password vault for each individual session, and the vault rotates each credential automatically once the session closes. Each month, Information Security reviews the privileged session logs for Velistra General Ledger and Corvessa Core Banking, matching recorded administrator activity to approved change tickets and opening an investigation into any activity that has no linked ticket. The reviewer signs and dates the completed log review, which is retained with the vault checkout and rotation reports and with notes documenting the investigation and resolution of each exception.

Each business day, the data center and cloud hosting operations team reviews the exception report covering administrator accounts and resolves or escalates every exception within two business days of the report date. Items that remain open beyond that window are aged and presented to management in a weekly summary for follow-up. The procedure carries out the enterprise escalation standard on privileged system access. Evidence retained includes the reviewed daily reports annotated with the disposition, resolution or escalation date for each exception, along with the weekly aged-item summaries sent to management.

Within Data Center & Cloud Hosting, a supervisor receives a report listing administrator accounts each month and reviews it, looking into any exceptions that exceed the established threshold before signing off on the report. The signed report is kept as evidence of the review, together with documentation of whatever follow-up actions resulted from exception investigation. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard that governs privileged system access.

Administrator credentials for each privileged session must be checked out of the password vault, and the vault rotates the password once the session closes, so no administrator keeps a standing credential. Each month, Information Security reviews the privileged session logs for Velistra General Ledger and Corvessa Core Banking and matches recorded activity to a linked change ticket. Any session without a corresponding ticket is investigated and followed up with the responsible administrator. The reviewer signs off on the monthly log extract and keeps it, along with investigation notes and resolution, as evidence for the general ledger and financial close process.

Within the general ledger and financial close process, the operations team reviews the daily exception report of administrator account activity each business day and works every flagged item. Each exception is either resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report, and the reviewer records the disposition, date and supporting rationale on the report. Items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aging summary and sent to management weekly, and the annotated daily reports and weekly summaries are retained as evidence of performance. This control carries out the enterprise escalation standard on privileged system access.

The process owner for general ledger and financial close approves the written procedures governing administrator accounts, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to staff. Each review is recorded with its date and the name of the approver. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is kept on file with the review evidence. These procedures put into practice the enterprise policy on privileged system access for this process area.

Information Security requires that administrator credentials for Velistra General Ledger and Corvessa Core Banking be checked out from the password vault for each individual session, and the vault rotates the credential automatically once the session ends. Each month, an Information Security analyst pulls the privileged session logs for both systems and matches every recorded session to a linked change ticket. Any session without a linked ticket is investigated with the responsible administrator and documented through to resolution. The analyst retains the monthly log extracts, the reconciliation to change tickets, and the investigation notes with sign-off as evidence; the control applies to the identity and access management process.

Each business day, the operations team reviews the exception report covering administrator accounts and documents a disposition for every item listed, as part of identity and access management. Each exception must be resolved or escalated within two business days. Any item still open past that window is reported to management in a weekly aged-items summary. The control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for privileged system access, and the annotated daily reports, escalation records, and weekly summaries are retained as evidence of performance.

Each month, the identity and access management supervisor reviews the administrator account report and investigates any exception above the established threshold, documenting the cause and the resolution for each item. After the review and follow-up are complete, the supervisor signs and dates the report to show it was reviewed. The signed report, exception investigation notes and records of any corrective actions, such as access removals or role changes, are kept as evidence for audit testing. This control carries out the requirements of the enterprise oversight standard governing privileged system access.

For each administrative session on Velistra General Ledger and Corvessa Core Banking, privileged administrator credentials must be checked out of the password vault and are automatically rotated once the session closes, so no administrator holds a standing password. Each month, Information Security pulls the privileged session logs for both systems and matches every session to a linked change ticket. Any activity without a ticket is investigated with the responsible administrator and documented through resolution. Evidence retained includes the vault checkout and rotation records, the monthly log extracts with the reviewer's sign-off and date, and investigation notes for each exception. This control is assigned to the IT operations and resilience area.

Each month, a supervisor within the IT operations and resilience function reviews the report of administrator accounts, investigates any exceptions that exceed the established threshold, and signs the report to attest that the review is complete. The signed report, along with documentation of the exception investigations and any resulting follow-up actions, is retained as evidence of the review. This control implements the enterprise oversight standard governing privileged system access.

The process owner within IT operations and resilience approves the written procedures governing administrator accounts, and these procedures put the enterprise policy on privileged system access into practice. The owner reviews the procedures at least annually and republishes the approved version to staff once each review is complete. Each version on file records the review date and the approver's identity, which serves as evidence of the annual review and approval. Any departure from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the procedure record.

Each year, brokerage operations staff who take part in access request approvals must complete role-specific training that carries out the enterprise learning requirement for user access provisioning. The brokerage operations manager tracks completion against the roster of approvers, and anyone past due loses the ability to act in the approval process until the training is done. Evidence kept for testing includes the annual completion report, the approver roster, and records showing when access was suspended and restored for overdue staff.

For in-scope online and mobile banking applications, each access request is raised in Okrin Identity Gateway and routed for approval to both the requesting user's manager and the application owner, and the system will not start provisioning until both approvals are recorded. Any request for access outside the role catalogue also needs Information Security sign-off before it moves forward. When a user changes role, Okrin Identity Gateway removes the prior access automatically. Evidence consists of the request and approval history held in Okrin Identity Gateway, including approver identity, timestamps, any Information Security sign-off for off-catalogue requests and the deprovisioning log entries for role changes, which Internal Audit samples during testing.

Each month, the supervisor responsible for the online and mobile banking function reviews the access request approvals report for that period and identifies any exceptions that exceed the established threshold. The supervisor investigates each such exception, documents the outcome and any remediation, and signs the report to evidence completion of the review. The signed report, together with supporting notes on follow-up actions, is retained as evidence of performance. This control is designed to meet the requirements of the enterprise oversight standard governing user access provisioning.

The process owner for online and mobile banking approves the written procedures that govern access request approvals and publishes the approved version to staff on the shared procedures site. The owner reviews the procedures at least annually and records the review date and the approver's identity on the document control page, so that each procedure traces back to the enterprise policy on user access provisioning that it implements. Any departure from the documented steps requires a written exception approval. Evidence retained includes the signed approval record, the annual review log, the publication notice to staff, and copies of approved exceptions.

Each quarter, Okrin Identity Gateway launches a recertification campaign covering user access to critical applications used by contact center operations. The assigned manager reviews every entitlement held by their staff and records a decision to certify or revoke it, and access marked for revocation is removed within five business days of the decision. Information Security monitors campaign progress and reports any campaign not completed to the Technology Risk Committee. Okrin Identity Gateway retains the campaign records, including manager decisions with timestamps and revocation completion dates, and Information Security keeps copies of its committee reporting as evidence.

Each business day, the contact center operations team works the daily exception report generated from entitlement reviews, researching every flagged access item and either resolving it or escalating it within two business days of the report date. Exceptions that remain open past that window are compiled into an aging summary and presented to contact center operations management on a weekly basis for review and direction. This procedure carries out the enterprise escalation standard for access recertification within the contact center function. Retained evidence consists of the annotated daily exception reports showing the disposition and date for each item, the escalation records, and the weekly aging summaries with management's documented review.

Each month, a designated analyst in contact center operations reconciles the balances and supporting records used in entitlement reviews back to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item that remains open beyond 30 days is escalated to contact center operations management, with the escalation date and planned resolution noted on the worksheet. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month end, and the signed worksheet, source system extract and escalation records are retained as evidence. This control puts into practice the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to access recertification.

Each quarter, Okrin Identity Gateway launches a recertification campaign covering all critical applications that support the general ledger and financial close process. Line managers review every entitlement assigned to their direct reports and either certify or revoke it, and the access administration team removes each revoked entitlement within five business days of the manager's decision. Information Security monitors campaign completion and reports any campaign not fully completed to the Technology Risk Committee. Okrin Identity Gateway retains the campaign completion reports, the manager certification and revocation decisions with timestamps, and the revocation closure records, and the Technology Risk Committee meeting materials retain the escalation reports.

Each month, a general ledger and financial close analyst reconciles the balances and records that support entitlement reviews back to the source system, as required by the enterprise balancing standard for access recertification. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated, and the escalation is noted on the reconciliation workpaper. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days. The signed workpaper, the source system extract, and the escalation record are retained as evidence for each monthly cycle.

Each quarter, Okrin Identity Gateway launches a recertification campaign for critical applications, and the responsible managers must either certify or revoke every entitlement assigned to their staff. Revoked access is removed within five business days of the manager's decision, and the gateway's campaign records and revocation tickets are kept as completion evidence. Information Security monitors campaign status and escalates any incomplete campaign to the Technology Risk Committee, with the committee reporting retained as support. The control falls within the identity and access management process.

Each month, an identity and access management analyst reconciles the balances and records supporting entitlement reviews back to the source system. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated to the function's management for resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer evaluates and signs the completed reconciliation within ten business days of month end. The signed reconciliation, the supporting extracts and the escalation records are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard for access recertification.

Within identity and access management, entitlement reviews are designed so that the employee who initiates a review cannot also approve it, and this split is enforced through role design rather than relying on manual practice. Each quarter, the identity and access management team runs a report of users who hold both the initiator and approver roles, reviews each flagged user, and removes the conflicting role. The team retains the quarterly report, its annotated review, and evidence of each role removal for audit inspection. This control puts into practice the enterprise separation-of-duties standard as it applies to access recertification.

Each business day, Quorvane Payments Hub automatically suspends any ACH file that would push an originator above its approved exposure limit, and a Payment Operations analyst reviews every suspended file before the processing window closes. A suspended file is released only after a second, independent Payment Operations approver also signs off. Separately, any originator whose return rate exceeds 0.5% is referred for an originator review. The control covers ACH operations, and the suspension queue, both approvals with user IDs and timestamps, and the originator review referrals are retained in the Quorvane Payments Hub audit trail as evidence of performance.

Within ACH operations, originator exposure entries are set up by one employee and approved by a different employee, and system role design prevents a single user from completing both steps on the same item. Each quarter, the ACH operations manager reviews a report of all users assigned both the initiation and approval roles, investigates each conflict, and has the conflicting access removed. The signed quarterly user report and the access removal tickets for every conflict are retained as evidence. This control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to ACH originations.

For originators in the commercial deposit services business, Quorvane Payments Hub automatically holds any ACH file that would push the originator past its approved exposure limit, and the file cannot settle until it is released. Each business day, Payment Operations reviews the held files against the originator's limit and current activity, and no file is released without the sign-off of a second approver who did not perform the initial review. Payment Operations also monitors originator return rates and opens a review of any originator whose returns exceed 0.5%. Evidence kept includes the suspended-file queue in Quorvane Payments Hub with reviewer and approver user IDs and timestamps for each release, along with documentation of any originator reviews triggered by the return-rate threshold.

Each month, a commercial deposit services analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records for ACH originator exposure to the source system, as the enterprise balancing standard for ACH originations requires. Any reconciling item open for more than 30 days is escalated, and the escalation is noted on the reconciliation alongside the item's age and status. A reviewer who did not prepare the reconciliation examines it and signs off within ten business days of month-end. The signed reconciliation, the supporting source system reports, and the escalation records are retained in the department's reconciliation file as evidence that the control was performed.

The Retirement Plan Recordkeeping process owner approves the written procedures governing originator exposure, which put into practice the enterprise policy on ACH originations, and makes sure the approved version is published where staff can reach it. The process owner reviews the procedures at least once a year, or sooner if a change to the ACH origination policy calls for an update, and logs the approver's name and the review date on the procedure document. Any departure from the procedures may proceed only after an exception approval has been documented. The approved procedure version, the review and approval record, and the file of exception approvals are kept as evidence for testing.

Within the retirement plan recordkeeping function, every employee whose role touches ACH originator exposure must complete role-specific training once each year, in line with the enterprise learning requirement governing ACH originations. The function's manager tracks completion against the annual deadline and has access to the origination process suspended for any employee who is overdue, restoring it only after the training is finished. The completion tracking report, the suspension and reinstatement requests, and the dated completion records are kept as evidence of the control's operation for the year.

Each quarter, the finance team runs the Calvane Credit Loss Model to estimate the allowance for credit losses and reconciles the loan balances used as model inputs to the Velistra General Ledger, investigating and clearing any differences before results are finalized. The team then presents the model output and every qualitative adjustment, each supported by written rationale, to the reserve committee, which reviews and approves the allowance before quarter-end close. Evidence kept for each quarter includes the signed balance reconciliation, the committee presentation with overlay rationale, and committee minutes recording the approval decision and any challenges raised.

Each month, Controller staff reconcile the balances and supporting records behind the current expected credit loss model output for the allowance for credit losses to the source system, investigating and documenting any differences. Reconciling items that remain open for more than 30 days are escalated for resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days, and the signed reconciliation, aging of open items and escalation records are retained as evidence. The control carries out the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to credit loss reserving.

Each quarter, finance staff run the Calvane Credit Loss Model and reconcile the loan balances used as model inputs to the Velistra General Ledger, with any differences investigated and cleared before results are finalized. Finance then presents the model output, along with each qualitative adjustment and its written rationale, to the reserve committee, which reviews and approves the reserve before quarter-end close. Evidence retained includes the signed balance reconciliation, the committee presentation package with overlay rationale, and committee minutes recording the approval decision. This control applies to the collections and recovery portfolio.

Access to the systems that support current expected credit loss model output for the collections and recovery function is provisioned only through approved roles, and each request must carry documented manager approval before it is granted. Each quarter, the collections and recovery manager recertifies all entitlements against current job responsibilities, and any access no longer needed is revoked. Access for leavers is removed within one business day of their separation date. The signed quarterly recertification reports, the approved access request tickets and the termination removal logs are kept as evidence that the control meets the enterprise access standard for credit loss reserving.

Each month, a collections and recovery analyst reconciles the balances and account records that feed the current expected credit loss model output back to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated to the unit's management with its age, amount and planned resolution noted. An independent reviewer signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days of month-end, and the signed worksheet, escalation log and supporting extracts are kept as evidence. This control carries out the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to credit loss reserving.

Within general ledger and financial close, the steps to initiate and to approve current expected credit loss model output are assigned to separate employees, and role design blocks any single user from completing both. Each quarter the Controller reviews a report of users who hold both the initiation and approval roles and has any conflicting access removed before the close is finalized. The signed report and records of each access removal are retained as evidence. This control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to credit loss reserving.

Each week, the AML operations team generates the open alert and case aging report from Tessaly Case Manager and reviews it to identify items outstanding beyond 30 days, which are escalated to the BSA Officer with a documented explanation for the delay and an expected disposition date. On a monthly basis, the QA team selects a 5% sample of closed alerts and independently re-performs the disposition review to confirm the closure decision was supported. The retained aging reports, escalation notifications to the BSA Officer, and QA sample worksheets with reviewer conclusions serve as evidence of performance for the BSA/AML program.

Each business day, the operations team works the exception report on BSA/AML alert disposition, reviewing every listed exception and either resolving it or escalating it within two business days of its appearance on the report. Items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aging summary and presented to management weekly. The control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for AML alert handling. Evidence retained includes the daily report annotated with the reviewer's initials, resolution notes and escalation dates for each exception, and the weekly aging summary with confirmation that management received it.

Under the BSA/AML Program, the analyst who initiates an alert disposition cannot also approve it, and role design in the alert workflow enforces this by keeping the preparer and approver entitlements with different employees, in line with the enterprise SoD standard as applied to AML alert handling. Each quarter, the BSA Officer or a delegate reviews a report of users who hold both the initiation and approval roles, and any conflicting access is removed. The quarterly user report, the reviewer's sign-off and date, and the access removal requests with their completion confirmations are retained as evidence of performance.

Corvessa Core Banking applies an automated activation hold to each new legal entity account opened through branch operations, and the hold stays in place until the onboarding team has completed and verified every beneficial ownership certification field. At account opening, the onboarding team reviews the certification, verifies the ownership information, and records its sign-off before the system will release the account for activity. Each night, the system recalculates customer risk ratings using current ownership and activity data. Evidence retained includes the system hold and release history for each account, the verifier's sign-off on the completed certification, and the nightly risk rating recalculation output.

The branch operations process owner approves the written procedures governing beneficial ownership files, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to branch staff on the procedures site. Each review records the review date and the approver's name on the procedure's version history page, and Internal Audit retains a copy of that page as evidence. Any departure from the procedure requires an exception approval, documented and kept with the related customer file. The procedure carries out the requirements of the enterprise CDD policy and cites that policy in its scope section.

Corvessa Core Banking enforces a system hold that keeps any new legal entity account from being activated until every beneficial ownership certification field is populated and the onboarding team has verified the information and recorded its sign-off. The hold is automated and runs at account opening, and an account can move to active status only once the onboarding verifier releases it. Customer risk ratings are recalculated nightly from ownership and activity data, so changes in ownership or account behavior feed into the rating without manual intervention. Evidence retained for testing under the BSA/AML program includes the account status history showing the hold and release dates, the onboarding verifier's sign-off on the certification fields, and the nightly risk rating job output.

Each business day, the operations team works the daily exception report for beneficial ownership files under the BSA/AML program, clearing each flagged item or escalating it within two business days of the report date. Exceptions that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged-item listing and presented to management weekly for review and direction. This follow-up carries out the enterprise escalation standard for customer due diligence (CDD). The retained evidence is the dated exception report annotated with the resolution or escalation date for each item, along with the weekly aged-item listing showing that management reviewed it.

Under the BSA/AML program, a designated supervisor reviews the monthly beneficial ownership file report shortly after it is produced and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold to determine its cause and the corrective action required. Once the review and investigations are complete, the supervisor signs the report to attest that it was examined. The signed report, exception investigation notes and records of follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for customer due diligence (CDD).

Corvessa Core Banking applies a systematic hold that prevents any new legal entity account within Commercial Deposit Services from being activated until the beneficial ownership certification fields are fully populated and the onboarding team has verified them. The onboarding team reviews each certification at account opening, records its verification in the system, and only then can the hold be released. Separately, customer risk ratings are recalculated nightly using ownership and activity data. Evidence retained includes the system hold configuration, the onboarding team's verification record for each account, and the nightly risk rating recalculation logs.

Within Commercial Deposit Services, beneficial ownership files are initiated by one employee and approved by a different employee, and role design prevents any single user from performing both steps. Each quarter, a report listing users who hold both the initiation and approval roles is generated and reviewed, and any conflicting access identified is removed. The reviewed quarterly report and the record of conflicts removed are retained as evidence of performance. This control puts into practice the enterprise separation-of-duties standard as it applies to customer due diligence.

For legal entity accounts opened through the digital account opening channel, Corvessa Core Banking applies a system hold that keeps the account inactive until the onboarding team has completed and verified every beneficial ownership certification field. An onboarding team member reviews the certification data before release, and the hold clears only when the system confirms that all fields are populated and marked verified. Customer risk ratings are then recalculated each night using the ownership and account activity data held in the system. Evidence retained includes the account status history showing the hold and release dates, the verifier's identity on the certification record, and the nightly risk rating recalculation job logs.

For digital account opening, the operations team reviews the daily exception report of beneficial ownership files each business day and either resolves or escalates every exception within two business days of its appearance on the report. Items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged exceptions summary and presented to management weekly. Reviewers record the disposition, the resolution or escalation date, and their initials for each exception on the retained daily report, and the weekly aged item summaries are kept with evidence of management review. This control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for CDD.

Corvessa Core Banking applies an automated activation hold to each new legal entity account opened through wealth client onboarding and will not release it until every beneficial ownership certification field is populated and the onboarding team has verified the entries against the certification provided by the customer. The onboarding team performs this verification before activation, and the system records the reviewer, the verification date and the time the hold was released in the account audit trail. Separately, customer risk ratings are recalculated nightly from ownership and activity data through an automated batch job. Retained evidence includes the hold and release logs, the completed certification records and the nightly batch run output showing the updated ratings.

Within wealth client onboarding, access to the systems that hold beneficial ownership files is provisioned only through approved roles, with Information Security granting entitlements on receipt of a manager-approved request that maps to a defined role. Each quarter, business line managers recertify every user's entitlements, and access that is no longer needed is revoked. Signed recertification attestations and the removal tickets are retained as evidence. When an employee leaves, access is removed within one business day of the termination notice, and the ticket timestamps are kept to show timeliness, consistent with the enterprise access standard governing CDD records.

Each month, a Wealth Client Onboarding supervisor reviews the beneficial ownership file report and checks the listed client files for complete ownership and control-person information. The supervisor investigates every exception above the established threshold, records the cause and the remediation steps, and signs and dates the report once the review is done. The signed report, together with notes on exception follow-up and any resulting corrective actions, is retained as evidence of performance. The control implements the enterprise oversight standard for customer due diligence as it applies to wealth onboarding.

Each year, BSA Compliance performs above- and below-the-line testing on every Merrow AML Monitor scenario and confirms that each product and channel in the BSA/AML program maps to at least one scenario. Any proposed threshold change takes effect only after the BSA Officer approves it and Model Risk completes validation. BSA Compliance retains the annual testing workpapers, the product and channel coverage mapping, the BSA Officer's signed approval of each threshold change, and the related Model Risk validation report as evidence of performance.

The BSA Officer, or a designated AML supervisor, reviews the monthly AML scenario tuning report for the BSA/AML Program. The review is completed each month after the report is produced. The reviewer investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold, records the disposition and any follow-up actions required, and signs the report to evidence completion. The signed report, the exception investigation notes, and documentation of follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control implements the enterprise oversight standard on transaction monitoring coverage.

The BSA Officer, as process owner for the BSA/AML Program, approves the written procedures governing AML scenario tuning, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to affected staff. These procedures put the enterprise transaction monitoring coverage policy into practice. Each review is logged with the review date and the name of the approver, and that record is retained alongside the approved procedure document. Any departure from the procedures may proceed only after an exception approval is documented, and the approval is kept as evidence for audit testing.

On an annual basis, BSA Compliance performs above- and below-the-line testing for each scenario configured in Merrow AML Monitor and maintains a coverage mapping showing that every product and channel, including real-time payments, is assigned to at least one scenario. Any proposed threshold change resulting from the testing must be approved by the BSA Officer and validated by Model Risk before it is implemented in production. Evidence retained includes the annual testing workpapers with sampled alert dispositions for each scenario, the signed product and channel coverage map, the BSA Officer's documented approval of each threshold change, and the corresponding Model Risk validation memo.

Each month, the real-time payments supervisor reviews the AML scenario tuning report, investigates every exception that exceeds the defined threshold, and documents the disposition of each item. After completing the review, the supervisor signs and dates the report to evidence that the work was done. The signed report, exception investigation notes, and records of any resulting follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control is how the business line meets the enterprise oversight standard for transaction monitoring coverage.

On an annual cycle, BSA Compliance performs above- and below-the-line testing for every scenario configured in Merrow AML Monitor, sampling alerts generated near the current thresholds and transactions falling just below them to confirm thresholds are set appropriately, and confirms that each product and channel, including remote deposit capture, is mapped to at least one active scenario. Any proposed threshold change requires BSA Officer approval and independent validation by Model Risk before it is implemented in production. Evidence retained for each annual cycle includes the testing workpapers and sample results, the product and channel coverage mapping, the signed BSA Officer approval for each threshold change, and the related Model Risk validation report.

Each month, a supervisor reviews the AML scenario tuning report for the remote deposit capture channel. The supervisor investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold and signs the report to show the review is complete. The signed report is retained with documentation of the investigations and any resulting follow-up actions, which serves as evidence that the control operates in line with the enterprise oversight standard for transaction monitoring coverage.

For Remote Deposit Capture, the process owner approves the written procedures that govern AML scenario tuning, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to staff so tuning work follows the enterprise policy on transaction monitoring coverage. Each review records the review date and the name of the approver on the procedure document's revision record, which is retained as evidence of the annual cycle. Any departure from the documented tuning steps must be supported by a written exception approval, and that approval is kept alongside the procedure for audit inspection.

For wire transfer operations, Brisance Wire Manager automatically screens each incoming and outgoing wire against the sanctions list, and no payment can be released until screening is complete. Sanctions list updates are loaded into the system automatically on their publication date, so screening always runs against the current list. When a wire generates a potential match, Compliance reviews the alert and records its disposition and rationale before the payment is either released or blocked. Evidence retained includes the system screening logs, the daily list load records, and Compliance's documented review of each potential match.

The wire transfer operations process owner approves the written procedures for OFAC hit review, reviews them at least annually against the enterprise sanctions screening policy they implement, and publishes the current version to staff. Each review is logged with its date and the approver's name, and the procedure document keeps a version history. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is kept with the procedure records as evidence for audit testing.

On an annual basis, the designated business continuity coordinator for each business unit, including branch operations, updates the unit's business impact analysis and continuity plan to reflect current critical processes, recovery time objectives, dependencies and staffing. After the refresh, the coordinator facilitates a tabletop exercise with process owners that walks through a disruption scenario affecting those critical processes and tests whether the plan is usable. Any gaps the exercise surfaces are logged in Orveth Change Manager with an assigned owner and target remediation date. Evidence retained includes the dated, approved business impact analysis and plan, the exercise attendance record and scenario summary, and the corresponding Orveth Change Manager entries showing each gap and its owner.

Each month, a branch operations supervisor reviews the report summarizing continuity exercises conducted across the branch network and investigates every exception that exceeds the defined threshold. After documenting the outcome of each investigation, the supervisor signs and dates the report to evidence completion of the review. The signed report, investigation notes and any resulting follow-up actions are retained as control evidence. This control is the branch operations procedure that implements the enterprise oversight standard on business continuity planning.

Each month, a designated branch operations staff member reconciles the balances and records that support business continuity exercises to the source system and documents any differences identified. Reconciling items that remain open for more than 30 days are escalated to branch operations management for resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month-end, and the signed reconciliation, supporting detail and escalation records are retained as evidence. This control implements the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to business continuity planning.

On an annual cycle, every business unit owning a critical process updates its business impact analysis and its continuity plan, confirming recovery priorities and dependencies against current operations. The same unit then facilitates a tabletop exercise that walks participants through a disruption scenario to test whether the refreshed plan holds up in practice. Any gaps identified during the exercise are logged in Orveth Change Manager with an assigned owner, and the updated analysis, plan, exercise notes and logged gap entries are retained as evidence for the business continuity management program.

Each month, a business continuity management supervisor reviews the report summarizing continuity exercises completed during the period and investigates any exception that exceeds the established threshold. After the review and any needed follow-up are complete, the supervisor signs the report to attest to it. The signed report is retained as evidence, together with documentation of the exception investigations and the resulting follow-up actions. The control implements the enterprise oversight standard for business continuity planning.

The business continuity management process owner approves the written procedures that govern continuity exercises, and these procedures carry out the enterprise policy on business continuity planning. The owner reviews them at least once a year and publishes the current version to staff in the procedures library. Each review is logged with its date and the approver's name. Any departure from the procedures during an exercise requires a documented exception approval, which is kept alongside the exercise records as evidence.

On an annual basis, the check processing business unit refreshes its business impact analysis and updates its continuity plan to reflect current dependencies, recovery time objectives, and staffing. Once the refresh is complete, the unit facilitates a tabletop exercise that walks participants through a disruption scenario affecting critical check processing activities. Gaps identified during the exercise are logged in Orveth Change Manager, each with an assigned owner and remediation target date. The updated analysis, the revised plan, the exercise attendance and scenario materials, and the Orveth Change Manager gap records are retained as evidence of performance.

The check processing owner approves the written procedures for continuity exercises, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to staff on the department's procedures page so it is available before each scheduled exercise. Each review records the review date and the approver on the document's revision history. Copies of the approved version are kept with the annual review sign-off as evidence. Any departure from the procedures during an exercise requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the exercise records. These procedures implement the enterprise policy on business continuity planning, and the owner confirms they remain consistent with that policy as part of each review.

Once a year, the payroll business unit refreshes its business impact analysis and its continuity plan so they reflect current processes, dependencies and recovery priorities. As part of the same annual cycle, payroll process owners and key staff run a tabletop exercise that walks through a disruption scenario against the updated plan. Gaps found during the exercise are logged in Orveth Change Manager, each with an assigned owner. The updated analysis, the revised plan, exercise attendance and notes, and the Orveth Change Manager gap entries with their owners are kept as evidence of performance.

Each month, a payroll analyst reconciles the balances and records that support continuity exercises back to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item that remains open for more than 30 days is escalated to payroll management and tracked until it is resolved. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month end, and the signed worksheet, the source system extracts and the escalation records are retained as evidence. This control carries out the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to business continuity planning.

On an annual basis, the business unit owner for real-time payments refreshes the business impact analysis and updates the continuity plan to reflect current recovery objectives, dependencies, and staffing. Following the refresh, the owner facilitates a tabletop exercise with key process participants that walks through a disruption scenario and tests whether the documented recovery steps remain workable. Each gap identified during the exercise is logged in Orveth Change Manager with an assigned owner and target remediation date. Retained evidence includes the dated business impact analysis and plan versions, the tabletop attendance record and scenario summary, and the corresponding Orveth Change Manager entries showing gaps and owners.

Each business day, the real-time payments operations team reviews the daily exception report generated from continuity exercises and works every item listed. Each exception is either resolved or escalated within two business days, and the reviewer records the disposition, date and any escalation path on the report. Exceptions that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged-item summary and presented to management each week. The signed daily reports and the weekly summaries are retained as evidence that the control operates under the enterprise escalation standard for business continuity planning.

The process owner for real-time payments approves the written procedures for continuity exercises, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to staff once each review is complete. Each review cycle records the review date and the approver's identity in the procedure's version history, which is retained as evidence of timely review and approval. Any deviation from the procedures may proceed only after an exception approval has been documented, and the approval is kept with the exercise records. These procedures put into practice the enterprise policy on business continuity planning for the real-time payments process.

Once a year, the finance team runs the capital stress test, using loss projections from the Calvane Credit Loss Model as the core credit inputs for the allowance for credit losses. Before the capital plan goes to the Board for approval, the chief risk officer's team acts as the second line and reviews and challenges the key scenario and loss assumptions, and finance must resolve or document a response to each challenge. Evidence retained includes the stress test results package, the second-line challenge log with finance responses and sign-off, and the Board minutes recording approval of the capital plan.

Within the Allowance for Credit Losses process, a supervisor performs a monthly review of the capital stress test report, examining results against established thresholds and investigating any exceptions that exceed them before signing off on the report. The signed report is kept as evidence of the review, together with documentation of exception research and any follow-up actions taken. This control implements the enterprise oversight standard governing capital adequacy planning.

For the allowance for credit losses process, every employee with a role in capital stress tests must complete role-specific training once each year, as required by the enterprise learning requirement on capital adequacy planning. The process owner tracks completion against the roster of participating staff and suspends process access for anyone who is overdue until they finish the assigned training. Retained evidence includes the annual completion report, the roster reconciliation, and records of access suspension and reinstatement for overdue staff.

Each year, finance performs the capital stress test, drawing on loss projections produced by Calvane Credit Loss Model and running them across the defined stress scenarios to estimate their effect on capital levels. Before the capital plan goes to the Board, the chief risk officer's team reviews and challenges the key assumptions, and finance must address or document each challenge raised. The Board then approves the capital plan, and the scenario results, the second-line challenge log with finance's responses, and the Board minutes recording approval are retained as evidence. This control covers the Treasury ALM function.

Each month a Treasury ALM supervisor reviews the capital stress test report and investigates any exception that exceeds the established threshold. The supervisor documents the cause and resolution of each exception, then signs the report to show the review is complete. The signed report, along with exception notes and records of any follow-up actions, is retained as evidence. This control puts into practice the enterprise oversight standard for capital adequacy planning.

Treasury ALM's process owner approves the written capital stress test procedures, which carry out the enterprise policy on capital adequacy planning. The process owner also reviews them no less than once a year and publishes the current version to staff once each review is complete. The record of each review shows the review date and the name of the approver. Any departure from the procedures may proceed only after an exception approval has been documented and retained with the procedure file.

Merrow Fraud Detection assigns real-time risk scores to card and online transactions, and this control covers the card disputes process. Each month, a fraud operations analyst pulls rule-level hit rates and associated fraud losses for the prior month and compares each rule's detection rate against its established target. Any rule with a detection rate below target is retuned, and the analyst documents the threshold or logic change, the rationale, and the post-change validation results. The monthly performance report, retuning log, and reviewer sign-off by the fraud operations manager are retained as evidence of performance.

Each business day, the card disputes operations team reviews the daily exception report on fraud rule performance and works every listed exception to resolution or escalation within two business days of the report date. Exceptions still open beyond that window are compiled into an aged-item summary that goes to management weekly for review and direction. The procedure carries out the enterprise escalation standard for card and account takeover, and the team keeps each daily report with reviewer initials, disposition notes and escalation dates, along with the weekly aged-item summaries, as evidence of performance.

Each year, the card disputes team lead confirms that every employee who takes part in fraud rule performance work has finished the role-specific training required under the enterprise learning standard for card and account takeover. Completion status is monitored against the team roster, and anyone past the due date has process access suspended until the training is complete. Evidence retained includes the annual completion report for the in-scope population, the list of overdue staff with the dates their access was removed and later restored, and the team lead's sign-off that the review was performed.

Merrow Fraud Detection assigns real-time risk scores to card and online transactions. Each month, the card fraud operations team reviews hit rates and associated fraud losses for every active rule. Any rule whose detection rate falls below the target is retuned, and the team documents the revised parameters and the rationale for each change. The monthly rule performance report, retuning log and reviewer sign-off are retained as evidence that the review was performed.

Each business day, the card fraud operations team works the daily exception report on fraud rule performance and documents a disposition for every exception it lists. Each exception must be resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report. Items that age past that window are compiled and reported to management weekly, consistent with the enterprise escalation standard for card and account takeover. Evidence retained includes the worked daily reports with analyst dispositions and dates, escalation records for unresolved items, and the weekly aged-item reports sent to management.

For the debit card program, Merrow Fraud Detection assigns a real-time fraud score to each card and online transaction. Each month, the fraud operations team pulls rule hit rates and fraud loss figures for the prior period and compares each rule's detection rate against its established target. Any rule that falls below target is retuned. The analyst records the proposed threshold or logic change, and a fraud operations manager approves it before it is deployed. The monthly performance report, the list of underperforming rules, the documented changes, and the evidence of approval are kept together as the review package for each cycle.

Each business day, the operations team supporting the debit card program reviews the daily exception report on fraud rule performance and works every listed exception to resolution or escalation within two business days of the report date. Exceptions that remain open past that window are compiled into an aging summary and presented to management weekly for direction on remediation. The procedure implements the enterprise escalation standard for card and account takeover. Evidence consists of the retained daily reports annotated with each exception's disposition, the reviewer's initials and the date worked, along with the weekly aging summaries sent to management, all kept for audit testing.

Each month, fraud operations analysts pull rule-level hit rates and confirmed fraud losses for card and online transactions that Merrow Fraud Detection scores in real time, covering the online and mobile banking channel. The analysts compare each rule's detection rate with its target and retune any rule that falls short, documenting the threshold or logic change and the reason for it. The fraud operations manager reviews and approves the results before retuned rules are promoted to production. Evidence retained for audit includes the monthly performance report, the list of rules below target with their before and after parameters, and the manager's dated sign-off.

Each month, a supervisor in the online and mobile banking function reviews the fraud rule performance report and investigates every exception above the established threshold. The supervisor signs the report to show that the review is complete. The signed report, the investigation notes and a record of any follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for card and account takeover within the online and mobile banking channel.

Each year, staff in online and mobile banking who support fraud rule performance complete role-specific training that carries out the enterprise learning requirement on card and account takeover. Business line management tracks completion against the population of assigned staff and removes process access for anyone who becomes overdue, restoring it only once the training is finished. Evidence retained includes the completion tracking records, a list of overdue staff for each cycle, and the dated access removal and reinstatement records for those individuals.

Each month, branch managers in branch operations perform unannounced surprise counts of teller drawers and vaults and reconcile the counted cash to the balances recorded in Corvessa Core Banking. During the same visit, the manager reviews the dual control access logs for the vault to confirm that every opening was attended by two authorized staff. Any shortage greater than $100 is escalated for follow-up. The signed count sheets, the reconciliation to the system balance, and the reviewed access logs are retained as evidence of performance.

The branch operations process owner approves the written vault dual control procedures, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to branch staff after each review. Each review cycle records the review date and the name of the approving process owner on the procedure document, and the dated approval is retained as evidence of the annual review. Any deviation from the dual control steps requires a documented exception approval, which is kept with the procedure file. The procedures implement the enterprise policy on cash custody, and the process owner confirms alignment with that policy during each review.

On an annual basis, branch operations management confirms that every employee who takes part in vault dual control has completed the role-specific training on cash custody required under the enterprise learning requirement. Branch operations tracks completion status throughout the year. Any employee whose training is overdue is removed from vault dual control duties and access until the training is finished. Evidence retained includes the annual training completion records, the overdue listings, and documentation of each access removal and later reinstatement, all kept for review.

Each month, on an unannounced date, the branch manager conducts a surprise count of every teller drawer and the vault and reconciles the counted totals to the balances in Corvessa Core Banking. During the same visit the manager reviews the dual control access logs for the vault to confirm that each opening was recorded with two authorized employees present. Any shortage greater than $100 is escalated, with the variance amount and explanation noted on the count record. The signed count sheets, the reconciliation to Corvessa Core Banking, and the reviewed access logs are retained at the branch as evidence for the cash management and vault process.

Each month, the Cash Management & Vault supervisor reviews the vault dual control report covering the prior period's vault openings, cash movements and custodian pairings. Any exception that exceeds the established threshold is investigated with the custodians involved, and the supervisor records the cause and the corrective action taken before signing and dating the report. The signed report, investigation notes and documentation of follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review, which carries out the enterprise oversight standard on cash custody.

Each year, all cash management and vault employees who take part in vault dual control must complete role-specific training that carries out the enterprise learning requirement on cash custody. The vault operations supervisor tracks completion against the current roster of dual control participants and, for any employee who is past due, removes them from the dual control rotation and suspends their vault access until the training is finished. The supervisor keeps the annual completion tracking report, the roster reconciliation, and records of each access suspension and reinstatement as evidence that the control operated.

On an annual basis, Treasury reviews the deposit runoff assumptions used in liquidity stress testing against observed recent stress events and the current level of uninsured deposit concentration, and records the rationale supporting each runoff rate. Market Risk independently challenges the proposed assumptions, and the assumptions are presented to ALCO for approval only after that challenge is documented and any points raised are resolved. Evidence retained includes the assumption comparison workpaper with rate rationale, the Market Risk challenge memo or email with Treasury responses, and the ALCO minutes reflecting approval, all filed with Liquidity Management documentation for the review year.

Each month, a liquidity management supervisor reviews the runoff assumptions report, investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold, and signs the report to evidence completion of the review. The signed report, together with documentation of exception research and any resulting follow-up actions, is retained as evidence of the control's performance. This supervisory review implements the enterprise oversight standard for liquidity stress scenarios.

Within liquidity management, runoff assumptions used in liquidity stress scenarios are entered by one employee and approved by a different employee, and role design prevents a single user from both initiating and approving the same assumption change. Each quarter, a report is generated listing all users who hold both the initiator and approver roles. Liquidity management reviews the report and removes any conflicting access it identifies. The signed review, the access report, and evidence of each role removal are retained to show compliance with the enterprise separation-of-duties standard as applied to liquidity stress scenarios.

Each business day, the Treasury ALM operations team reviews the exception report on runoff assumptions and either resolves or escalates every item within two business days of it appearing. Exceptions that remain open past that window are reported to management in a weekly aged-items summary. The team keeps the annotated daily report, showing the disposition, the reviewer's initials, and the date each exception was cleared or escalated, along with the weekly summaries sent to management. This control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for liquidity stress scenarios.

Once a year, Treasury executes a small-dollar test draw against each contingent funding source, including the FHLB advance line and the Federal Reserve discount window, to confirm that access works in practice. As part of each draw, Treasury reconciles pledged collateral values with the lending counterparty and logs the elapsed time from request to receipt of funds. A summary of results, any failed or delayed steps, and the remediation owners and target dates is presented to ALCO and retained with the committee minutes and draw confirmations as evidence. The control sits within the liquidity management process.

Each year, the liquidity management team lead confirms that every employee who takes part in backup funding line tests has completed the required role-specific training. The lead reviews the completion tracking report against the current list of test participants. Any staff member whose training is overdue is removed from the testing process and regains access only after finishing the course. The completion report, the participant roster, and records of any access removals and reinstatements are retained as evidence that the enterprise learning requirement on contingency funding readiness is met.

Orveth Change Manager enforces a system control that prevents any production deployment from proceeding until the associated change ticket shows completed testing and recorded approval, and the tool's role configuration prevents developers from deploying code they authored. For emergency changes that bypass the standard pre-deployment approval path, the change board performs a retrospective review within two business days of implementation, documenting its conclusion and any follow-up actions on the ticket. Evidence retained for change management includes the ticket history in Orveth Change Manager, with testing sign-off, approver identity and timestamps, deployment logs showing the deploying user differs from the developer, and the change board's dated review notes for each emergency change.

The process owner for change management approves the written procedures that govern change tickets and reviews them at least annually to confirm they still implement the enterprise policy on production changes. After each approval, the procedures are published to staff so that personnel raising and working change tickets follow the current version. The procedure document records each review date and the name of the approver as evidence of the annual review. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the related change ticket.

Each month, a change management analyst reconciles the balances and records behind production change tickets to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Reconciling items that remain open more than 30 days are escalated, with the escalation date and status noted on the worksheet. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, and the signed worksheet, supporting extracts and escalation records are kept as evidence. The control applies the enterprise balancing standard to production changes.

Orveth Change Manager acts as an automated preventive control for the data center and cloud hosting environment, holding every deployment until the associated change ticket shows completed testing and a recorded approval. System permissions enforce segregation so that developers cannot promote their own code to production, and a separate individual must carry out each release. When an emergency change is pushed through ahead of normal approval, the change board performs a retrospective review within two business days of implementation. The ticket history, approval and test records, deployment logs, and change board review notes are kept in Orveth Change Manager as evidence of control operation.

Each month, a data center and cloud hosting operations analyst reconciles the balances and records behind production change tickets to the source system, under the enterprise balancing standard for production changes. Any reconciling item open longer than 30 days is escalated to the team manager for resolution, and its status is tracked until it clears. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines and signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days of month-end. The signed reconciliation workpaper, the source system extract and the escalation log are retained as evidence.

Each year, every staff member in the data center and cloud hosting function who raises, reviews, approves or implements change tickets completes training specific to that role. This training satisfies the enterprise learning requirement for production changes. IT management tracks completion status against the annual deadline and removes change process access from anyone who is overdue, restoring it only after the training is finished. Completion records, overdue listings and evidence of each access removal and reinstatement are retained to support the annual cycle.

For the digital account opening application, Orveth Change Manager blocks any deployment to production until the associated change ticket shows completed testing and documented approval. Developers cannot deploy their own code, and the tool enforces this separation by preventing the ticket requester from also executing the release. Emergency changes that bypass the standard path are reviewed by the change board within two business days after implementation, and the board records its review outcome and any follow-up actions on the ticket. Evidence retained includes the ticket approval and testing history, deployment logs, and change board review records, all kept within Orveth Change Manager.

On a monthly basis, the digital account opening supervisor reviews the change ticket report covering production changes made to the process during the prior month. Any exception exceeding the established threshold is investigated, with the cause and resolution noted, and the supervisor signs the report once the review is complete. The signed report, together with documentation of investigations and any resulting follow-up actions, is retained as evidence of performance. This control operates in support of the enterprise oversight standard governing production changes.

Each month, a change management analyst supporting the digital account opening process reconciles the balances and records behind change tickets to the source system and documents any differences in the monthly reconciliation workpaper. The analyst escalates any reconciling item that remains open longer than 30 days, noting the escalation date and the owner assigned to resolve it. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, and the signed workpaper, supporting source system extracts and escalation records are retained as evidence. This control applies the enterprise balancing standard to production changes.

Within IT operations and resilience, Orveth Change Manager prevents any production deployment from proceeding until the associated change ticket shows completed testing and a recorded approval. Developers are restricted from deploying their own code, so a separate individual must release each approved change. When an emergency change is pushed through ahead of normal approval, the change board reviews it after the fact within two business days and documents its conclusion on the ticket. Evidence retained includes the ticket history with test results and approval timestamps, deployment logs showing the releasing user differs from the developer, and change board minutes or sign-offs for each emergency review.

Each month, an IT operations and resilience supervisor reviews the change ticket report for production changes, investigates every exception that exceeds the defined threshold, and records the outcome and any required follow-up against the relevant tickets. When the review is complete, the supervisor signs and dates the report to show it was performed. The signed report, investigation notes and evidence that follow-up actions were completed are retained for audit. This control puts into practice the enterprise oversight standard governing production changes.

For changes to the online and mobile banking applications, Orveth Change Manager prevents any deployment from proceeding until the associated change ticket shows completed testing and recorded approval. The tool also enforces segregation of duties so that developers are unable to deploy code they authored. When an emergency change is deployed outside the standard approval path, the change board performs a retrospective review within two business days of deployment. The change tickets serve as evidence of the control and are retained in Orveth Change Manager, including test results, approver identity and timestamps, deployer identity, and the change board's documented emergency review.

The process owner for online and mobile banking approves the written procedures that govern change tickets, which put the enterprise policy on production changes into practice for that channel, and publishes the approved version where staff can reach it. At least annually, the process owner reviews the procedures, revises them as needed and records the review date and the approver's name with the published document. Any departure from the procedures may proceed only with a documented exception approval, which is kept alongside the related change ticket as evidence for testing.

Each month, a designated analyst in the online and mobile banking team reconciles the balances and records that support change tickets back to the source system, which carries out the enterprise balancing standard for production changes. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated, and the escalation is logged with the item's age and status. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month-end. The signed reconciliation, the source system extract it was built from, and the escalation log are kept as evidence of performance.

On each business day, Corvessa Core Banking automatically screens every deposited item received through branch, mobile and remote capture channels against items already presented across all three channels to identify potential duplicates. When an item is flagged as a suspected duplicate, the system places a hold on it and routes it to fraud operations staff, who review the item and decide whether to release the hold or escalate it before funds become available. This control supports the check processing function, and evidence retained includes the system-generated duplicate exception report, the hold records with timestamps, and the reviewer's documented disposition for each flagged item.

Each month, check processing management measures the duplicate item detection indicator and compares the result to its defined threshold, in line with the enterprise indicator framework for check fraud. When the indicator breaches the threshold, management escalates it to the risk committee along with a documented action plan and a named owner responsible for remediation. Evidence retained includes the monthly indicator reports with threshold comparisons, the escalation materials submitted to the risk committee, and the related action plans showing the assigned owner and status.

Each year, the check processing supervisor confirms that every employee who performs or reviews duplicate item detection has completed the role-specific training required under the enterprise learning requirement on check fraud. The supervisor reviews the completion tracking report against the current roster of staff assigned to the process and identifies anyone past the annual due date. Any employee found overdue has access to duplicate item detection suspended until the training is finished, and the supervisor confirms completion before restoring access. Evidence retained includes the reviewed completion report with the supervisor's sign-off, the list of overdue employees, and the access suspension and reinstatement records for each of them.

For deposits within commercial deposit services, Corvessa Core Banking automatically compares every deposited item against items received through the branch, mobile and remote capture channels to identify potential duplicates. When an item matches a previously presented item, the system places a hold on the suspect item and routes it to fraud operations, which reviews each held item on the business day it is flagged and decides whether to release the hold or return the item. The system retains a record of each duplicate match and hold, and fraud operations documents its review decision, reviewer and date against the held item as evidence of performance.

Each month, commercial deposit services management calculates the duplicate item detection indicator and compares the result to the defined threshold set for that measure. When the result exceeds the threshold, management escalates the breach to the risk committee with a remediation action plan, a named owner and a target completion date. This review applies the enterprise indicator framework for check fraud to the commercial deposit line. Management retains the monthly indicator worksheet, the documented threshold comparison and, for any breach, the escalation memo and the committee minutes recording the action plan and owner.

As each item is deposited, Corvessa Core Banking automatically checks it against items already presented through the branch, mobile and remote capture channels to identify potential duplicates. When an item is flagged as a suspected duplicate, the system places a hold on it and routes it to the fraud operations team, who review it daily and either release the hold or escalate the item for return or further investigation. Evidence retained includes the system-generated duplicate exception and hold log and the reviewer's documented disposition and date for each held item, and the control is scoped to the remote deposit capture process.

Each month, management responsible for the remote deposit capture channel measures the duplicate item detection indicator and compares the result to its defined threshold. Any breach is escalated to the risk committee along with a remediation action plan and an assigned owner, and the item is tracked until closure. The monthly indicator results, threshold comparisons, escalation submissions, and committee minutes recording the action plan and owner are retained as evidence. The control is how the remote deposit capture channel applies the enterprise indicator framework for check fraud.

Credit Administration maintains a covenant tickler in Halbrook Loan Origination that tracks financial statement due dates for each construction lending relationship and flags items that are past due. Within 30 days of receiving the borrower's financial statements, a credit analyst calculates the required covenants and records the results against the loan file. Any breach or proposed waiver is escalated to the credit officer, who approves or declines it and reviews whether the risk rating should change. Evidence retained includes the tickler report, the covenant calculation worksheet with its completion date, and the documented credit officer approval and risk rating review, all kept in Halbrook Loan Origination.

Each business day, the construction lending operations team reviews the exception report for borrower financial statement tracking and works every listed item, documenting the resolution or escalation within two business days of the item first appearing. Exceptions that remain open beyond that window are compiled into an aged items summary and presented to management weekly, and management's review is evidenced by sign-off on the summary. The team retains the worked daily reports, annotated with disposition notes, dates and preparer initials, along with the weekly aged items summaries, as evidence of performance. This control operates as the business line's implementation of the enterprise escalation standard on covenant compliance.

The construction lending process owner approves the written procedures for tracking borrower financial statements, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes each approved version to staff on the department's procedures site. Every review records the review date and the approver's name on the document's revision history page, which serves as the retained evidence of the annual review. Any departure from the procedures must have a documented exception approval kept with the related loan file, and the procedures map to the enterprise policy on covenant compliance, which they put into practice.
