For the commercial real estate lending portfolio, Credit Administration maintains a tickler in Halbrook Loan Origination that records when each borrower's financial statements are due and flags items that are outstanding. Within 30 days of receiving the statements, a Credit Administration analyst calculates the required covenants and documents the results in a covenant compliance worksheet attached to the loan record. Any covenant breach or waiver request goes to the credit officer, who approves or declines it and reassesses the loan's risk rating. Evidence retained includes the tickler status report, the dated covenant calculation, and the credit officer's signed approval with the rating review notes.

Each month, a commercial real estate lending operations analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used for financial statement tracking back to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Reconciling items that remain open beyond 30 days are escalated to lending management with an explanation and expected resolution date. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, and the signed worksheet, supporting source system extracts and escalation records are retained as evidence. This control carries out the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to covenant compliance.

Within commercial real estate lending, the employee who initiates a financial statement tracking entry cannot be the same employee who approves it, and role design enforces this separation so that no single user can complete both steps. Each quarter, the lending operations manager reviews a report of users assigned both the initiation and approval roles, removes any conflicting access, and retains the signed report and access removal confirmations as evidence. This control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to covenant compliance monitoring.

Credit Administration analysts maintain a tickler in Halbrook Loan Origination that records the due date of each borrower financial statement required under the loan agreement, and they follow up on any submission that becomes past due. Within 30 days of receiving a statement, the analyst calculates each applicable covenant, records the result and supporting worksheet in Halbrook Loan Origination, and notes whether the borrower is in compliance. Any covenant breach or proposed waiver is escalated to the responsible credit officer, who approves or declines the waiver and determines whether the loan's risk rating should be reviewed and changed. Evidence retained for each review includes the tickler entry with its received date, the covenant calculation, and the credit officer's documented approval and risk rating review.

Within Credit Administration, role design ensures that one employee initiates each financial statement tracking entry and a different employee approves it, so no individual can complete both steps for the same borrower record. Each quarter, a Credit Administration manager reviews a report of all users who hold both the initiation and approval roles, removes any conflicting access found, and documents the reason for each removal. The signed quarterly report and the record of access removals are retained as evidence that this control operates as required by the enterprise separation-of-duties standard on covenant compliance.

For loans in the middle market lending portfolio, Credit Administration maintains a tickler in Halbrook Loan Origination that tracks each borrower's financial statement due dates and flags items that are approaching or past due. Within 30 days of receiving the statements, a Credit Administration analyst calculates the required covenants and records the results against the loan record. Any covenant breach or proposed waiver goes to the responsible credit officer, who decides on approval and reviews whether the borrower's risk rating should change. Evidence retained in Halbrook Loan Origination includes the tickler status, covenant calculation worksheets with receipt and completion dates, and the credit officer's documented approval and rating conclusion for each exception.

Each month, middle market lending management measures the financial statement tracking indicator for the portfolio against its defined threshold and records the result. Any breach is escalated to the risk committee along with an action plan and a named owner responsible for remediation. The control puts the enterprise indicator framework into practice for covenant compliance. Evidence retained includes the monthly indicator calculation, the threshold comparison, and, for breaches, the escalation materials and risk committee minutes showing the assigned owner and action plan.

Within middle market lending, the employee who initiates a financial statement tracking entry cannot also approve it, and this separation is enforced through access role design rather than manual oversight. Each quarter, a report listing any users who hold both the initiation and approval roles is generated and reviewed, and every conflicting assignment identified is removed. The reviewed report, documentation of each conflict and its removal, and reviewer sign-off are retained as evidence. The control carries out the enterprise separation-of-duties standard as it applies to covenant compliance.

Each year the independent loan review function selects a risk-based sample of commercial and consumer credits and re-grades every sampled credit without relying on the risk rating assigned by Credit Administration. Reviewers record their assigned grade, supporting rationale, and any rating disagreement on a standardized review worksheet for each credit. All disagreements are compiled into a summary report and delivered to the Chief Credit Officer. Credit Administration must book any agreed downgrade within 30 days, and the review worksheets, the summary report, and evidence of the rating change are retained as support for the control.

Each month, a Credit Administration analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used in rating migration back to the source system and documents any differences on the reconciliation worksheet. Reconciling items that remain open beyond 30 days are escalated, and the escalation is noted on the worksheet with the item age and current status. A Credit Administration reviewer independent of the preparer signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days of month-end, which evidences review and approval. The control applies the enterprise balancing standard to credit risk grading, and the signed worksheets and escalation records are retained for Internal Audit testing.

Each year, Credit Administration requires every employee who takes part in rating migration to complete role-specific training on credit risk grading, which satisfies the enterprise learning requirement for that subject. Credit Administration management tracks completion against the roster of in-scope staff and suspends an overdue employee's access to rating migration activities until the training is finished. Evidence retained includes the annual completion tracking report, records of access suspensions and reinstatements for overdue staff, and the current roster of in-scope employees.

On an annual basis, the independent loan review function selects a risk-based sample of commercial and consumer credits and re-grades each one independently of the originating lender and relationship manager. Any difference between the assigned risk rating and the loan review rating is documented and reported to the Chief Credit Officer for resolution. Agreed downgrades must be recorded in the loan file and reflected in the bank's books within 30 days of the review conclusion. Retained evidence includes the sample selection rationale, individual re-grade worksheets, the rating disagreement report delivered to the Chief Credit Officer, and documentation showing the date each downgrade was booked. This control is owned and performed by loan review.

Within Loan Review, the operations team works the daily rating migration exception report each business day, researching each flagged item against the enterprise escalation standard for credit risk grading. Each exception must be resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report. Items that remain open beyond that window are compiled into an aging summary and presented to management weekly. The team keeps the annotated daily reports, along with the escalation records and the weekly aging summaries, as evidence of performance.

Each month, a loan review analyst reconciles the balances and underlying records that support rating migration back to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Reconciling items that remain open beyond 30 days are escalated to loan review management, and the escalation and its resolution status are noted on the worksheet. A designated reviewer independent of the preparer signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days of month-end. The worksheet, supporting source extracts, escalation records and reviewer sign-off are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard for credit risk grading.

Once a year, the independent loan review function selects a risk-based sample of credits from the middle market lending portfolio and re-grades each one without reference to the line's assigned rating. Every rating disagreement is reported to the Chief Credit Officer, and any downgrade that results must be booked within 30 days of that report. Retained evidence includes the sample selection rationale, the re-grade worksheet for each credit, the disagreement report delivered to the Chief Credit Officer, and documentation showing the date each downgrade was booked.

Each month, a Credit Administration analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records behind middle market lending rating migration to the source system, documents each variance, and keeps the completed reconciliation workbook with the supporting extracts. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated, and the escalation notice is attached to the workbook along with its current status. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, and the dated sign-off is kept as evidence that the control was performed. The control carries out the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to credit risk grading.

Contact center operations staff and branch personnel enter every customer complaint, including those received verbally at a branch, into Tessaly Case Manager no later than one business day after receipt, recording the intake date, channel and complaint category. Each day the Complaints Manager reviews the open-case aging in Tessaly Case Manager and takes ownership of escalation for any complaint that has remained unresolved for more than 15 days, documenting the follow-up actions and target resolution date in the case record. Each month the Complaints Manager prepares an aging summary of complaints open beyond 15 days for the Compliance Committee. Evidence retained includes the Tessaly Case Manager case history and timestamps, escalation notes, the monthly aging report and the Compliance Committee meeting minutes showing the report was presented.

Each year, every contact center operations employee who logs complaint cases must finish role-specific training, as the enterprise learning requirement on complaint resolution directs. The contact center operations supervisor tracks completion against the roster of staff assigned to complaint case logging and identifies anyone past the annual due date. Overdue employees have their access to the complaint logging process suspended until they finish the training, and the supervisor confirms completion before restoring access. The completion tracking report, records of each access suspension and reinstatement, and the supervisor's sign-off are kept as evidence that the control operated.

The process owner for customer complaints management approves the written procedures governing complaint case logging, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to all staff who log complaint cases. Each review is evidenced by the recorded review date and the name of the approver, and both are retained with the procedure document. Any deviation from the documented steps requires an exception approval, which is documented and kept on file. The procedure carries out the requirements of the enterprise policy on complaint resolution, and reviewers confirm that alignment during the annual review.

Mortgage servicing staff record every complaint they receive, verbal complaints taken at branches included, in Tessaly Case Manager no later than one business day after receipt. Each day the Complaints Manager reviews the aging report from Tessaly Case Manager, and any complaint still unresolved after 15 days is escalated to the Complaints Manager so it can be followed up and a resolution path documented. Every month the Complaints Manager reports the open and escalated items to the Compliance Committee. Evidence retained includes the case records with intake and escalation timestamps, the aging reports, and the monthly Compliance Committee reporting package along with its meeting minutes.

Each month, mortgage servicing management measures the complaint case logging indicator and compares the result to its defined threshold, as required by the enterprise indicator framework for complaint resolution. When the result breaches the threshold, management escalates it to the risk committee with a documented action plan and a named owner responsible for remediation. Evidence retained for audit includes the monthly indicator report showing the measured value against the threshold, the escalation submission for any breach, and the committee minutes recording the action plan and assigned owner.

Within Mortgage Servicing, the employee who logs a complaint case cannot also approve it, and role design enforces the split. Each quarter, servicing operations management reviews a report of users holding both roles, removes any conflicts and keeps the signed-off report as evidence. This control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to complaint resolution.

On a quarterly basis, Compliance extracts complaint data for card disputes from Tessaly Case Manager and analyzes it by product, channel and complaint theme to identify recurring issues. Any theme that exceeds the established threshold is assigned to a root cause owner, who is responsible for determining the underlying cause and defining corrective actions. Compliance tracks each corrective action through to closure and retains the quarterly analysis, the owner assignments and the action tracking records with closure evidence as support for the control.

Within card disputes, the Complaints Manager grants access to the systems that support complaint root cause analysis only through approved roles, and each request and approval is kept on file. Each quarter, the Complaints Manager recertifies all entitlements and retains the signed recertification and any resulting removals as evidence. When an employee leaves, their access is removed within one business day, and the termination notice and removal date are kept to show timeliness. This procedure carries out the enterprise access standard as it applies to complaint trend analysis.

Each month, an analyst on the card disputes team reconciles the balances and records supporting complaint root cause data to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item that has remained open for more than 30 days is escalated, and the escalation date and reason are recorded on the worksheet. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation, follows up on open items, and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed worksheet, source system extracts and escalation records are retained as evidence that the control operates under the enterprise balancing standard for complaint trend analysis.

Each quarter, Compliance extracts complaint data from Tessaly Case Manager and analyzes it by product, channel and theme as part of consumer compliance monitoring. Any theme that exceeds the established threshold is assigned a root cause owner, who is responsible for identifying the underlying cause and agreeing on corrective actions. Compliance tracks each corrective action to closure and retains the quarterly analysis, the threshold exception listing with assigned owners, and the action tracking log showing status and closure evidence.

Each business day, the operations team reviews the exception report on complaint root causes generated for consumer compliance monitoring and works every listed exception to resolution or escalation within two business days of the report date. Items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged exception summary and presented to management each week for review and direction. As required by the enterprise escalation standard on complaint trend analysis, the team keeps the annotated daily report showing each exception's disposition, reviewer initials and date, along with the weekly aged summary and evidence of its delivery to management.

For complaint root cause analysis under consumer compliance monitoring, role design ensures that one employee initiates a root cause determination and a different employee approves it, so no single user can complete both steps. Each quarter, a report listing any users who hold both the initiation and approval roles is generated and reviewed. Any conflicting access identified is removed, and the report is retained with sign-off and evidence of removal. The control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to complaint trend analysis.

Each quarter, Compliance extracts complaint data from Tessaly Case Manager and analyzes volumes and trends by product, channel and theme as part of the customer complaints management process. For any theme that exceeds the established threshold, Compliance assigns a root cause owner and records the resulting corrective actions, then tracks them through to closure in later quarters. Evidence retained includes the quarterly analysis workbook, the threshold comparison showing which themes were flagged, the owner assignments, and the corrective action log with status updates and closure support.

Each month, a supervisor in customer complaints management reviews the report summarizing complaint root causes and investigates any exception that exceeds the defined threshold. Once the review is complete and any needed follow-up is assigned, the supervisor signs and dates the report. The signed report, investigation notes and documentation of follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for complaint trend analysis within the complaints management process.

The process owner for customer complaints management approves the written procedures covering complaint root causes, which implement the enterprise policy on complaint trend analysis, and publishes the approved version to staff. These procedures are reviewed at least annually, and each review is logged with the review date and the name of the approver to evidence completion. Any departure from the procedures must be supported by a documented exception approval, which is retained with the procedure file for audit inspection.

Within the collections and recovery function, Haskett Collections automatically prioritizes delinquent accounts in the work queue by days past due and outstanding balance. Each business day, collections supervisors review the queue aging report and identify any account that has not been contacted within five days of entering its delinquency bucket. Supervisors reassign those accounts to an available collector and record the reassignment and the reason in Haskett Collections. The daily aging report, initialed by the reviewing supervisor, and the reassignment history in Haskett Collections are retained as evidence of performance.

Within collections and recovery, role design ensures that the employee who initiates an action on a collection queue cannot also approve it, so maker and checker duties always rest with different people. Each quarter, collections and recovery management runs a report of users holding both the initiation and approval roles, reviews each conflict, and has the conflicting access removed. The signed-off quarterly report and evidence of the access removals are retained as support for the review. This control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to delinquency management activity.

Each business day, collections supervisors supporting the credit card underwriting portfolio review the queue aging view in Haskett Collections, where accounts are ranked by days past due and outstanding balance. Any account that has gone five days without a contact attempt since entering its current delinquency bucket is reassigned to another collector for immediate follow-up. Supervisors retain the daily aging report with their review date and initials, along with the reassignment log showing the original and new collector for each escalated account.

Within Credit Card Underwriting, a supervisor reviews the monthly collection queues report after it is produced at month-end. The supervisor investigates each exception above the defined threshold and documents the follow-up actions taken. The supervisor then signs the report to attest that the review is complete. The signed report, the exception investigation notes and the record of follow-up actions are retained as evidence, consistent with the enterprise oversight standard on delinquency management.

Each month, an analyst in the credit card underwriting function reconciles the balances and account records supporting the collection queues to the source system and documents any differences as reconciling items. Any reconciling item open longer than 30 days is escalated to management for resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed reconciliation, supporting reports and escalation records are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard for delinquency management.

Haskett Collections ranks delinquent accounts in the mortgage servicing collections queue by days past due and outstanding balance so that higher-risk accounts surface first. Each business day, collections supervisors review the queue aging view and identify any account that has gone five days without a contact attempt since entering its current delinquency bucket. The supervisor reassigns each such account to another collector and records the reassignment in Haskett Collections. Evidence consists of the daily queue aging report bearing the supervisor's review sign-off and the reassignment history kept in the system.

Each month, a mortgage servicing supervisor reviews the collection queue report, which summarizes delinquent loan activity across the servicing collection queues. The supervisor investigates every exception that exceeds the defined threshold, records the cause and any follow-up actions, and signs and dates the report once the review is complete. The signed report, exception notes and evidence of follow-up are retained with the monthly servicing records for audit inspection. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard on delinquency management for the mortgage servicing function.

Each month, mortgage servicing staff reconcile the balances and supporting records behind the collection queues to the source system and document any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item that remains open beyond 30 days is escalated for resolution, with the escalation noted on the worksheet. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines and signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days. The signed worksheet, supporting source system extracts, and escalation records are retained as evidence of operation, consistent with the enterprise balancing standard as applied to delinquency management.

Each business day, a collections supervisor for Small Business Lending reviews the delinquency queue aging in Haskett Collections, where accounts are prioritized by days past due and outstanding balance. Any account with no contact within five days of entering its delinquency bucket is reassigned by the supervisor to another collector for prompt follow-up. The daily aging review and the resulting reassignments are recorded in Haskett Collections, and the system's account assignment history is retained as evidence of the review.

The Small Business Lending process owner approves the written procedures that govern collection queues and reviews them at least once a year, or sooner if workflows change. After approval, the current version is published to staff. The procedures carry out the enterprise policy on delinquency management. Each review records the approver's name and the review date as evidence. Any departure from the procedures must have a documented exception approval, which is retained with the procedure file.

Each year, the small business lending collections manager confirms that every employee assigned to the collection queues has completed the role-specific training required under the enterprise learning requirement on delinquency management. Completion status is monitored throughout the cycle, and any employee who passes the due date without finishing has queue access removed until the training is completed. Restoration of access is approved by the manager only after completion is confirmed. The annual completion report, records of each access removal and reinstatement, and the manager's sign-off are retained as evidence of performance.

On an annual basis, human resources submits each incentive plan covering brokerage operations to risk and Compliance, which review the plan design for features that could encourage inappropriate sales or conduct risk and document their conclusions and any required changes. Before payouts are released from Quillon HR and Payroll, human resources reduces or withholds amounts tied to reversed sales and to conduct findings raised during the performance period. Evidence retained includes the signed annual review memo from risk and Compliance, the adjustment worksheet reconciling gross to net payouts by employee, and the approval record for the final payout file loaded to Quillon HR and Payroll.

Within brokerage operations, access to the systems used to process payout adjustments is provisioned only through predefined roles that have been approved by the business owner, and Information Security grants no entitlement outside those roles. Each quarter, brokerage operations management recertifies all user entitlements and documents removals or changes. When an employee leaves, access is revoked within one business day of the termination notice, and the signed recertification packages and revocation tickets are kept as evidence. This control puts into effect the enterprise access standard on incentive plan design.

Each year, human resources submits every incentive compensation plan to risk management and Compliance, which review the plan design for features that could encourage inappropriate sales or conduct. Before each payout cycle is released from Quillon HR and Payroll, human resources reduces individual awards for sales later reversed and for conduct findings, and a second reviewer validates the reductions. Evidence retained includes the annual review sign-off from risk management and Compliance, the adjustment worksheet showing each reversed sale and conduct finding applied, and the approved payout register exported from Quillon HR and Payroll.

On a monthly basis, the incentive compensation supervisor reviews the payout adjustments report for the period, comparing each adjustment against the supporting plan calculations and approvals. Any adjustment exceeding the established threshold is treated as an exception and investigated, with the supervisor documenting the cause and the resolution or follow-up action required. Once the review is complete, the supervisor signs the report, and the signed report, together with the exception investigation notes and records of follow-up actions, is retained as evidence. This control operates to satisfy the enterprise oversight standard governing incentive plan design.

The payroll process owner approves the written procedures that govern payout adjustments, and these procedures carry out the enterprise policy on incentive plan design. At least once a year the process owner reviews the procedures and confirms they are still current, then republishes the approved version so staff can reach it. Each review is recorded with the date and the approver's name, and that record is kept with the procedure document as evidence. Any payout adjustment handled outside the documented steps needs a written exception approval, which is retained alongside the related payroll records.

Each quarter, portfolio management extracts funded balances and unfunded commitments from Ylvara Data Warehouse and prepares a commercial real estate concentration report that breaks out exposure by property type and market. The preparer compares each concentration against the limits approved by the Board, flags any category in breach, and escalates every breach to the Board Risk Committee with the exposure amount and the limit exceeded. The control covers the construction lending portfolio, where undrawn commitments can materially increase exposure. The quarterly report, the data warehouse extract used to build it, the limit comparison worksheet, and the escalation package sent to the Board Risk Committee are kept as evidence of performance.

Each business day, the construction lending operations team reviews the daily exception report generated for commercial real estate limit reporting and works every exception listed on it. Analysts must resolve each exception or escalate it within two business days, and they record the disposition, the date and the reviewer's initials on the report. Any exception that remains open past that window is carried to an aged-items summary that goes to management every week. The signed daily reports, escalation correspondence and weekly aged-item summaries are retained as evidence that the control operates under the enterprise escalation standard on property concentration.

Within construction lending, commercial real estate limit reporting is prepared by one employee and approved by a different employee, and role design prevents the same person from performing both steps. Each quarter, Credit Administration runs a report of users holding both the initiation and approval roles, reviews it, and removes any conflicting access it finds. The reviewer signs and dates the report and keeps it with evidence of each access removal as the record of the review. This control carries out the enterprise SoD standard as it applies to property concentration.

Each quarter, the portfolio management team runs a concentration report from Ylvara Data Warehouse that breaks out funded balances and unfunded commitments on commercial real estate lending by property type and by market. The team measures each segment's combined exposure against the concentration limits approved by the Board and documents the comparison in the quarterly limit review. Any limit breach is escalated to the Board Risk Committee, along with the exposure amounts and the affected property types or markets. The finalized report, the limit comparison and evidence of escalation to the Board Risk Committee are kept as the quarterly control record.

Each month, a supervisor in the commercial real estate lending unit reviews the limit report for commercial real estate exposures, investigates every exception above the established threshold, and signs the report once those exceptions are resolved or escalated. The signed report, notes on each exception investigated, and records of any follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard on property concentration.

Within commercial real estate lending, limit reporting is split so that one employee initiates each report and a different employee approves it, a separation enforced through role design rather than manual oversight. Each quarter, Credit Administration reviews a report of users holding both the initiator and approver roles and removes any conflicting access it finds. The reviewer signs and dates the quarterly report, and it is retained with evidence of each conflict removed. The control implements the enterprise SoD standard as it applies to property concentration.

For the data center and cloud hosting environment, the security operations team triages each high-severity alert within one hour of generation, continuously across all shifts. The analyst assigned to the alert opens a record in Tessaly Case Manager that captures the alert details, investigative steps, conclusion, and timestamps showing triage was started within the one-hour window. When the investigation confirms an incident, the analyst escalates it under the incident response plan and records the escalation and the receiving party in the same case. Tessaly Case Manager retains the case records, alert timestamps, and escalation notes as evidence of performance.

Each business day, the data center and cloud hosting operations team reviews the daily exception report generated from security alert triage and works every listed item. Each exception is either resolved or escalated within two business days, and the analyst records the disposition, the date and any escalation path on the report. Items that age past that window are compiled into a weekly summary for management review, and the signed reports and weekly summaries are retained as evidence of performance. This control puts into practice the enterprise escalation standard for cyber threat detection.

For the real-time payments environment, the security operations team reviews and triages each high-severity alert within one hour of generation, applying the same standard to alerts raised outside business hours. Analysts open a record in Tessaly Case Manager for every such alert and capture the time of triage, the steps taken to investigate, the conclusion reached, and the analyst responsible. When an alert is confirmed as an incident, the team escalates it in line with the incident response plan and notes the escalation time and recipients in the same case record. The case records, with their timestamps and attached investigation notes, are retained as evidence that the control operated.

Each business day, the operations team supporting real-time payments works the daily exception report generated for security alert triage. Analysts must resolve or escalate every exception within two business days. Any items aged beyond that window are compiled and reported to management on a weekly basis. This procedure carries out the enterprise escalation standard for cyber threat detection, and the team retains the dated exception reports with disposition notes and the weekly aging summaries as evidence of performance.

The real-time payments process owner approves the written procedures for triaging security alerts, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to staff who perform triage. Each review is logged with its date and the name of the approver. Any departure from the procedures must be covered by a documented exception approval, which is kept with the procedure file. The procedures put the enterprise cyber threat detection policy into effect for real-time payments, and evidence includes the approved procedure document, the review log and any exception approvals.

For wire transfer operations, the security operations team reviews each high-severity alert and completes initial triage within one hour of the alert firing. The analyst records the investigation steps, findings and disposition in a Tessaly Case Manager case linked to the alert. Any alert the analyst confirms as an incident is escalated under the incident response plan, and the escalation time and recipient are logged in the same case. The retained case records, including alert and triage timestamps, serve as evidence for testing the one-hour standard and the escalation decision.

Each business day, the wire transfer operations team works the daily exception report generated from security alert triage, and each exception is either resolved or escalated within two business days of its appearance on the report. On a weekly basis, the team compiles any exceptions that remain open past the two-day window into an aged-item summary, which goes to operations management for review and direction. The control implements the enterprise escalation standard for cyber threat detection. Evidence retained includes the annotated daily exception reports showing the resolution or escalation of each item, the analyst's initials and date, and the weekly aged-item summaries with management's acknowledgment.

Each business day, Ylvara Data Warehouse automatically executes completeness and validity rules against the critical data elements supporting Credit Administration. Any records failing these rules are written to an exception report. Each month, the designated data owners review the accumulated exceptions, determine root cause, and sign off on the review. Remediation actions and their status are logged in Tessaly Case Manager, and the signed exception reports together with the case records are retained as evidence of performance.

Each business day, the Credit Administration operations team reviews the exception report produced by the data quality rules and works every flagged item. An exception has to be either resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report. Items that age past that window are compiled and sent to Credit Administration management on a weekly basis. This follows the enterprise escalation standard for critical data quality, and the team retains the annotated daily reports and the weekly aged-item summaries as evidence.

Each month, a Credit Administration analyst reconciles the balances and records that feed the data quality rules back to the source system, in line with the enterprise balancing standard for critical data quality. The analyst investigates any reconciling item that remains open beyond 30 days and escalates it to Credit Administration management for resolution. Within ten business days of month end, an independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off on it. The signed reconciliation workbook, the supporting source extracts, and the escalation log are kept as evidence of performance.

Each day, Ylvara Data Warehouse automatically runs completeness and validity rules against the critical data elements in scope for the data governance function and flags any records that fail. Every month, the responsible data owners review the accumulated exceptions, decide on the cause and corrective action for each, and sign off on their review. Remediation steps and owner sign-off are logged in Tessaly Case Manager, which serves as the retained evidence alongside the daily rule execution results kept in Ylvara Data Warehouse.

Each month, data governance management calculates the key risk indicator for data quality rules and compares the result with the defined threshold set under the enterprise indicator framework for critical data quality. When the indicator breaches the threshold, management escalates it to the risk committee together with a remediation action plan and a named owner. Evidence retained includes the monthly indicator calculation, the threshold comparison, and the escalation package with committee minutes showing the action plan and owner assignment.

Each day, Ylvara Data Warehouse automatically runs completeness and validity rules against the critical data elements that feed regulatory reporting and flags any records that fail. Once a month, the assigned data owners review the accumulated exceptions, decide on corrective action, and sign off on their review. Remediation steps and their status are logged as cases in Tessaly Case Manager. The daily rule execution logs, the monthly exception reports bearing owner sign-off, and the related case records are kept as evidence of performance.

Each business day, the regulatory reporting operations team reviews the exception report produced by the data quality rules and resolves or escalates every exception within two business days of it first appearing. Any item still open past that window is treated as aged and summarized for management in a weekly report. Evidence of each resolution or escalation, along with a copy of the weekly aged-item summary, is kept so that timeliness can be tested. The control puts into practice the enterprise escalation standard for critical data quality.

Each month, a regulatory reporting analyst reconciles the balances and records that feed the data quality rules back to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated to regulatory reporting management, with the escalation date and its owner recorded on the worksheet. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, and the signed worksheet, supporting extracts and escalation notes are retained as evidence. This control carries out the requirements of the enterprise balancing standard for critical data quality.

Each day, Ylvara Data Warehouse automatically runs completeness and validity rules against the critical data elements that support regulatory reporting data and flags any record that fails a rule as an exception. Each month, the designated data owners review the accumulated exceptions, determine root cause, and sign off on the disposition of each item. Remediation actions, owner sign-off, and target dates are recorded in Tessaly Case Manager. The daily rule execution logs and the monthly exception reports are retained as evidence of performance.

Each business day, the operations team reviews the exception report produced by the data quality rules over regulatory reporting data and works every flagged item. Each exception must be resolved or escalated within two business days, and the team records the root cause, corrective action, and disposition date against the item in the exception log. Items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged-item summary and presented to management weekly, with the distribution email and management's acknowledgment retained as evidence. This procedure implements the enterprise escalation standard for critical data quality, and the daily report, exception log, and weekly summaries are kept for audit testing.

Each month, the regulatory reporting data analyst reconciles the balances and record counts that feed the data quality rules for regulatory reporting data back to the source system, investigating and documenting any differences. Any reconciling item that remains open beyond 30 days is escalated to the reporting manager for resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed reconciliation, the aging schedule of reconciling items and the escalation record are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard for critical data quality.

Card disputes staff log each consumer error claim in Tessaly Case Manager when it is received, and the system records the applicable regulatory deadlines on the case. Unless the investigation has been completed by day ten, Tessaly Case Manager automatically posts provisional credit to the customer's account on that day. A supervisor in the card disputes function reviews open cases daily against their deadlines and follows up on any approaching the day ten mark. The case record, including intake date, deadline fields, investigation notes and the provisional credit posting entry, is retained in Tessaly Case Manager as evidence of performance.

The card disputes process owner approves the written procedures governing provisional credit on consumer error claims, reviews them at least annually against the enterprise policy they implement, and publishes the current version to disputes staff. Each review records the review date and the approver's name on the procedure's version history. Any departure from the procedures must be supported by a documented exception approval, which is kept with the related dispute file. The evidence retained for testing is the approved procedure document, its version history showing review dates and approvers, proof of publication to staff, and the exception approvals issued during the period.

For consumer error claims arising from check processing, Deposit Operations staff open a case in Tessaly Case Manager on the day each claim is received. The case records the claim details and the applicable regulatory deadlines. If the investigation has not been completed by day ten, the system automatically posts provisional credit to the customer's account. Deposit Operations reviews open cases daily against their deadlines. Evidence retained includes the case record with intake date, deadline fields, investigation notes and the system log of any provisional credit posting.

Within deposit account servicing, staff enter every consumer error claim into Tessaly Case Manager on the day it is received, recording the claim date and the regulatory deadlines that apply to it. If the investigation has not been completed by day ten, the system automatically posts provisional credit to the customer's account. Any claim closed before day ten is resolved without provisional credit, and the case record documents the completion date and outcome. Tessaly Case Manager retains the evidence for each claim, including the case intake record, deadline fields, investigation notes and the system entry for any provisional credit posting.

Each month, a deposit account servicing supervisor reviews the provisional credit report and investigates any exception that exceeds the established threshold. The supervisor signs the report to show the review is complete. The signed report is retained with notes on each exception investigated and any follow-up actions taken. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for consumer error claims.

The Deposit Account Servicing process owner approves the written provisional credit procedures, which implement the enterprise policy on consumer error claims. The owner reviews them at least annually and publishes the current version to servicing staff. Each review is evidenced by a recorded review date and approver name, which Internal Audit can inspect against the published version. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, and that approval is retained with the procedure record.

Deposit Operations staff record each consumer error claim in Tessaly Case Manager when it is received, and the system assigns the applicable regulatory deadlines to the case. If the investigation is not complete by day ten, Tessaly Case Manager automatically posts provisional credit to the customer's account, and staff monitor open cases daily against their deadlines. This control covers claims within the escheatment and dormant accounts process. Evidence retained includes the case record with its intake date and deadlines, the system audit trail of the provisional credit posting, and the investigation closure notes.

The process owner for escheatment and dormant accounts maintains written procedures governing provisional credit and approves them before they are published to staff, who can access the current version. At least once a year, the process owner reviews the procedures against the enterprise policy on consumer error claims, which they implement, and records the review date and approver name on the procedure document. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval before it proceeds. Evidence retained for testing includes the approved procedure version showing the recorded review date and approver, proof of publication to staff, and copies of any exception approvals issued during the period.

For online and mobile banking channels, Deposit Operations staff record each consumer error claim in Tessaly Case Manager on receipt, and the system assigns the applicable regulatory deadlines to the case. If the investigation has not been closed by day ten, Tessaly Case Manager automatically posts provisional credit to the customer's account without manual intervention. Deposit Operations reviews the open-case queue daily to confirm that deadlines are tracked and that automated credits have posted as expected. Evidence retained includes the case record with intake date, deadline fields, investigation status and closure notes, along with the system log showing the date and amount of any provisional credit posted.

The online and mobile banking process owner approves the written provisional credit procedures, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the approved version to staff. These procedures put into effect the enterprise policy governing consumer error claims. Each review records the review date and the approver's identity, and the dated, approved procedure is retained as evidence. Any departure from the procedure requires a documented exception approval, which is kept with the procedure file.

Each year, every online and mobile banking employee with a role in provisional credit on consumer error claims completes training specific to that role, as the enterprise learning requirement for those claims directs. The business line's training coordinator tracks completion against the roster of in-scope staff and flags anyone who misses the annual deadline. Overdue employees have their access to the provisional credit process removed and regain it only after they finish the training. Completion reports, the in-scope roster, and records of each access removal and reinstatement are retained as evidence.

Each week, Treasury runs a report from Pellmark Liquidity Manager listing the top 50 depositors and their uninsured balances for the commercial deposit services portfolio. The Treasury analyst compares each depositor's balance and the aggregate uninsured position against the approved concentration triggers and notes any breach on the report. Any trigger breach is escalated to ALCO with the depositor detail and the size of the exceedance. The signed weekly report, the trigger comparison worksheet, and the escalation email or memo to ALCO are retained in the Treasury shared drive as evidence of performance.

The commercial deposit services process owner approves the written procedures for top depositor tracking, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to staff so that tracking activity follows the enterprise policy on large depositor concentration that the procedures implement. Each annual review records the review date and the approver's name, and that record is kept with the approved procedure version as evidence. Any departure from the documented steps proceeds only after an exception approval is documented, and the approved exception is kept with the procedure file for audit testing.

Each week, Treasury runs a report from Pellmark Liquidity Manager listing the top 50 depositors by balance along with total uninsured balances. The Treasury analyst checks the results against the approved depositor concentration triggers. When a breach is found, it is escalated to ALCO with a short note covering the affected relationships and the size of the exceedance. The control sits within Liquidity Management. Treasury keeps the weekly report, the documented trigger comparison, and any escalation correspondence to ALCO as evidence of performance.

Access to the systems used for top depositor tracking in liquidity management is granted only through approved roles. Each request is validated against the role catalog before provisioning, and Treasury management reviews and recertifies all entitlements quarterly, with retained sign-offs and records of any access removed as a result. Information Security removes access for leavers within one business day of separation and keeps the termination ticket, timestamped removal confirmation and quarterly recertification file as evidence. The control implements the enterprise access standard as it applies to large depositor concentration.

Each week, Treasury runs a report from Pellmark Liquidity Manager that lists the top 50 depositors and their uninsured balances for the online and mobile banking channel. The Treasury analyst compares each concentration measure against the established early warning triggers and notes on the report whether any trigger has been breached. When a breach is found, Treasury escalates it to ALCO with a short explanation of the depositor exposure and its movement since the prior week. The signed weekly report, the trigger comparison worksheet and any escalation emails to ALCO are retained in the Treasury shared folder as evidence of performance.

The process owner for online and mobile banking approves the written procedures for top depositor tracking, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to staff in the line of business. Each review is logged with the review date and the name of the approver, and the prior version is retained so that changes between cycles can be traced. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is kept with the procedure file. The procedures put into practice the enterprise policy on large depositor concentration, and the approved document, review log and exception approvals serve as evidence of the control.

Each business day, Ostrand Treasury Workstation automatically marks every interest rate derivative position to market and measures the resulting exposure against approved counterparty limits and collateral thresholds. Where a threshold is exceeded, the system generates a margin call in its workflow queue, and operations staff review and issue the call to the counterparty on the same day. The daily valuation run log, the exposure-versus-threshold comparison output, and the issued margin call records with timestamps are retained in Ostrand Treasury Workstation as evidence of performance.

Each month, a Treasury analyst reconciles the balances and records that support margin calls on interest rate derivatives to the source system and investigates any differences in swap counterparty exposure. Any reconciling item that remains open for more than 30 days is escalated, and the escalation is noted on the reconciliation workpaper along with the item's age and its planned resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days of month end. The signed workpaper, supporting system extracts and escalation records are kept as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard.

Each year, staff who take part in margin calls for interest rate derivatives must complete role-specific training that implements the enterprise learning requirement on swap counterparty exposure. Treasury management monitors completion against the roster of in-scope personnel. Anyone past the annual deadline has their access to the margin call process suspended until the course is complete. The completion reports, the overdue listings, and records of each access removal and reinstatement are kept as evidence that the control operated.

Once each year, IT performs an end-to-end failover of every critical service supporting card production and fulfillment, bringing the upstream and downstream dependencies into the exercise rather than testing the service alone. During the test the team logs actual recovery times for each service and compares them to the approved recovery objectives. Any gap between achieved and targeted recovery is opened as a remediation item in Orveth Change Manager and tracked to closure. The retained evidence consists of the test plan, the timed recovery results set against objectives, and the related Orveth Change Manager records showing remediation status.

Each month, card production and fulfillment management calculates the failover testing risk indicator and compares the result to its defined threshold, recording the value and the breach status in the monthly indicator log. When the indicator breaches the threshold, management escalates it to the risk committee, presenting an action plan with an assigned owner and a target remediation date. The control applies the enterprise indicator framework to system recovery capability. Retained evidence includes the monthly indicator log, threshold comparison worksheets, escalation submissions to the risk committee, and the related committee minutes showing the action plan and owner.

Technology performs an end-to-end failover of every critical service once a year, and each test includes the upstream and downstream dependencies that the service relies on or feeds. For each service, the test team records the actual recovery time and compares it with the approved recovery objective, noting any shortfall. Each gap is opened as a remediation item in Orveth Change Manager and tracked there through closure. Retained evidence includes the test plan and execution log, the recovery time comparison, and the linked Orveth Change Manager records, all filed under the IT operations and resilience control area.

Each business day, the IT operations team reviews the exception report generated from failover testing and assigns an owner to every exception listed. Within two business days, each exception is either resolved or escalated, and the analyst records the disposition, the date and any supporting notes against the item on the report. Once a week, items that have aged past that window are compiled and presented to IT operations and resilience management, and the weekly summary and annotated daily reports are kept as evidence of review. The control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for system recovery capability.

Within IT operations and resilience, failover tests must be initiated by one employee and approved by a different employee, and this split is enforced through role design so that neither step can be completed by the person who performed the other. Each quarter, IT operations and resilience management generates a report of all users holding both the initiation and approval roles, reviews each instance, and removes the conflicting access. The reviewer's sign-off on the quarterly report and the access removal records for any conflicts are retained as evidence. The control applies the enterprise SoD standard to the bank's system recovery capability.

Technology performs an end-to-end failover exercise once a year for each critical service supporting online and mobile banking, bringing its upstream and downstream dependencies into scope so the full service chain is exercised. During each test, the team records actual recovery times and compares them with the established recovery objectives, noting any service or dependency that falls short. Each gap identified is logged and tracked to remediation in Orveth Change Manager. Retained evidence includes the annual test results with recorded recovery times versus objectives and the related Orveth Change Manager remediation records.

Each month, the online and mobile banking supervisor reviews the failover testing report and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold, documenting the cause and the remediation agreed with the responsible team. The supervisor signs and dates the report once all exceptions above threshold have been resolved or assigned a follow-up owner and target date. The signed report, investigation notes and records of follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control implements the enterprise oversight standard on system recovery capability for the online and mobile banking channel.

For online and mobile banking, initiating a failover test and approving it are assigned to separate roles by design, so the same employee cannot perform both steps. Each quarter, the application access owner generates a report listing any user who holds both the initiation and approval roles, reviews it, and removes the conflicting access, recording the remediation date for each case. The signed quarterly report and the supporting access removal tickets are retained as evidence. This control puts the enterprise separation-of-duties standard into effect for system recovery capability.

Each quarter, Compliance extracts pricing exception data for Consumer Mortgage Lending from Ylvara Data Warehouse and performs a disparity analysis to identify pricing outcomes that differ across borrower groups. Compliance confirms that a documented reason supports every pricing exception in the population and follows up on any exception lacking adequate justification. Outliers identified in the analysis are reviewed with the line of business, and the conclusions and any required actions are recorded. The quarterly analysis workpapers, exception rationale testing results, and documentation of outlier review discussions are retained as evidence of performance.

Each month, a consumer mortgage lending operations analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used in pricing exception reviews back to the source system, then investigates and documents any differences found. Reconciling items that remain open beyond 30 days are escalated to lending management with a note on cause and expected resolution. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month-end. The signed reconciliation workpaper, aging schedule of open items, and escalation records are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard on equitable pricing.

Each quarter, Compliance pulls pricing exception data for credit card underwriting from Ylvara Data Warehouse and performs a disparity analysis to identify pricing differences across applicant groups. Every pricing exception must carry a documented reason, and Compliance follows up on any exception lacking one until it is supported or escalated. Statistical outliers identified in the analysis are reviewed with credit card underwriting line of business management to confirm whether the variance is justified. Compliance retains the quarterly data extract, the analysis workpapers, exception reason documentation and minutes or notes from the outlier review meeting as evidence of performance.

Each month, a designated analyst in Credit Card Underwriting reconciles the balances and supporting records used in pricing exception reviews back to the source system. The analyst investigates any break, documents it on the reconciliation workpaper, and escalates every reconciling item that has been open for more than 30 days. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, and the signed workpaper and escalation log are kept as evidence. The control carries out the enterprise balancing standard as it applies to equitable pricing.

Annually, each credit card underwriting employee who takes part in pricing exception reviews must complete role-specific training that carries out the enterprise learning requirement on equitable pricing. The underwriting manager monitors completion status against the roster of staff assigned to pricing exception reviews and identifies anyone who has not finished by the due date. Overdue staff have their access to the pricing exception review process removed and regain it only after completing the training. Evidence retained includes the annual completion report, the assigned-staff roster, and records of access suspensions and reinstatements for overdue employees.

Each quarter, Compliance pulls pricing exception data for home equity lending from Ylvara Data Warehouse and performs a disparity analysis to identify pricing differences that may indicate inconsistent or unfair treatment of borrowers. Every exception in the population must carry a documented reason, and Compliance follows up on any exception that lacks adequate support. Compliance then reviews statistical outliers with the line of business to confirm whether a legitimate business justification exists or whether remediation is needed. Evidence retained includes the quarterly data extract, the analysis workbook, exception rationale documentation, and meeting notes recording the outlier review and its resolution.

The home equity lending process owner approves the written procedures that govern pricing exception reviews, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to staff so that loan officers and reviewers work from the same instructions. Each review cycle records the review date and the name of the approver on the procedure document, and that record is kept as evidence that the annual review happened. Any departure from the procedures is allowed only with a documented exception approval, which is retained with the related review file. These procedures put into effect the enterprise policy on equitable pricing for the home equity lending line.

Each month, a Home Equity Lending analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used in pricing exception reviews back to the source system and documents any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item outstanding longer than 30 days is escalated for resolution, with the escalation date and owner noted on the worksheet. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed worksheet, escalation records and supporting reports are retained as evidence that the control was performed under the enterprise balancing standard for equitable pricing.

Each quarter, Compliance extracts pricing exception data for Small Business Lending from Ylvara Data Warehouse and performs a disparity analysis to identify pricing patterns that may indicate unfair treatment. Every pricing exception in the population must carry a documented business reason, and Compliance follows up on any exception lacking one before the analysis is finalized. Outliers identified in the results are reviewed with line of business management to confirm or remediate the pricing decisions. Evidence retained includes the quarterly data extract, the completed analysis workpapers, exception reason documentation, and records of the outlier review discussions with the line of business.

Each month, a small business lending supervisor reviews the report summarizing that period's pricing exception reviews and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold. Once the investigation is complete, the supervisor signs the report to attest that the review was performed. The signed report, along with documentation of any follow-up actions taken on the investigated exceptions, is retained as evidence of the control's operation. This control implements the enterprise oversight standard on equitable pricing for the small business lending portfolio.

Within the estate settlement function, Information Security provisions access to the systems used for trust account reviews only through predefined roles approved by the estate settlement manager, and requests that fall outside an approved role are rejected. Each quarter, the estate settlement manager recertifies all user entitlements against current job duties, and Information Security removes or adjusts any access flagged during the review. When a staff member leaves, their access is revoked within one business day of the separation notice. Evidence retained includes approved access request tickets, signed quarterly recertification reports with remediation notes, and termination logs showing revocation dates, all in support of the enterprise access standard on fiduciary administration.

Within personal trust administration, trust officers perform an annual review of every account maintained in Tarrance Trust Accounting, assessing investment holdings against the governing instrument and investment objectives, confirming that distributions made during the period were authorized and properly supported, and verifying that required account documents are current and on file. Each completed review is documented in a signed review worksheet with the reviewer's conclusions and any follow-up items, and the review completion date is recorded in Tarrance Trust Accounting. Each month, the fiduciary committee receives a report of accounts whose annual review is past due, discusses the reasons for delay and assigns target completion dates. Committee minutes and the monthly overdue review report are retained as evidence of that oversight.

Each business day, the personal trust administration operations team works the exception report generated for trust account reviews, investigating every flagged item and either resolving it or escalating it within two business days of the report date. Items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged exceptions summary and presented to management weekly. The operations team retains the annotated daily report, notes on how each item was resolved or escalated, and the weekly aged item summary with management's acknowledgment as evidence of performance. This control puts into practice the enterprise escalation standard as it applies to fiduciary administration.

The personal trust administration process owner approves the written procedures that govern trust account reviews, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to staff in the department's procedures library. Each review is logged with its date and the name of the approver, and the prior version is kept to show what changed. Any departure from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the review record. These procedures carry out the enterprise policy on fiduciary administration, and the annual review checks that they remain aligned with that policy.

Trust officers perform an annual review of every retirement plan recordkeeping account maintained in Tarrance Trust Accounting, assessing investment holdings, distribution activity and compliance with governing account documents. Each completed review is documented on a signed review form, with follow-up actions for any exceptions noted, and retained in the account file. Each month the fiduciary committee reviews a report of accounts whose annual review is past due and records its discussion and any required remediation in its meeting minutes.

In Retirement Plan Recordkeeping, the employee who initiates a trust account review cannot be the one who approves it, and role design in the access model enforces this split. Each quarter, a report listing every user who holds both the initiator and approver roles is generated and reviewed, and any conflicting access is removed. The reviewed report and the records of access removal are kept as evidence. The control puts the enterprise separation-of-duties standard into effect for fiduciary administration activities.

Payment Operations monitors the Federal Reserve account balance continuously through the real-time intraday position dashboard in Pellmark Liquidity Manager throughout each business day, including Real-Time Payments activity. Whenever the projected intraday position falls below the established floor, Payment Operations staff hold large outgoing payment releases and escalate to Treasury, and the held items are not released until Treasury grants approval. Evidence retained includes the dashboard position snapshots captured at the time of each breach, the hold log identifying the affected payments, and the documented Treasury approval for each release.

Each business day, the operations team supporting real-time payments reviews the exception report on the Federal Reserve account balance and works every flagged item to resolution or escalation within two business days. For each exception, the reviewer records the cause, the action taken and the disposition date on the report. Unresolved items are escalated under the enterprise escalation standard on intraday funding. Aged exceptions are summarized and sent to management weekly, and the annotated daily reports and weekly aging summaries are retained as evidence of performance.

Each month, the real-time payments supervisor reviews the report of the Federal Reserve account balance and investigates every exception that exceeds the defined threshold. Once all exceptions are resolved or have documented follow-up actions, the supervisor signs and dates the report to evidence completion. The signed report, the investigation notes and records of any follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard on intraday funding for the real-time payments activity.

Payment Operations staff supporting wire transfer operations monitor the Federal Reserve account balance throughout the business day using the real-time intraday position dashboard in Pellmark Liquidity Manager. Before each large outgoing payment is released, the operator checks the projected intraday position. If the release would bring that position below the established floor, the operator places the payment on hold and does not release it until Treasury grants approval. Evidence includes the dashboard position history, the hold and release records for affected payments, and Treasury's documented approval, all retained in Pellmark Liquidity Manager for audit testing.

Each business day, the wire transfer operations team reviews the exception report on the Federal Reserve account balance and works every listed item. Each exception is resolved or escalated within two business days, in line with the enterprise escalation standard for intraday funding. Exceptions still open past that window are compiled into an aging summary and presented to management weekly. The annotated daily report, escalation records, and weekly aging summaries are retained as evidence of performance.

Within wire transfer operations, activity affecting the Federal Reserve account balance is initiated by one employee and approved by a different employee, and role design prevents a single user from completing both steps. Each quarter, a report of users who hold both the initiation and approval roles is generated and reviewed, and any conflicting access found is removed. The reviewer retains the signed-off quarterly report with notes on each conflict and the date it was removed. This control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to intraday funding activity.

Each month, Treasury runs the rate shock report in Pellmark ALM for the interest rate derivatives portfolio and checks the result of every scenario against the limits approved by the board. Any limit breach is escalated to ALCO within five business days of identification. It is also presented to the Board Risk Committee at the committee's next scheduled meeting, together with a remediation plan that names the corrective actions and target dates. Treasury keeps the signed-off monthly report, the limit comparison, the ALCO escalation notice and minutes, and the Board Risk Committee materials and minutes as evidence of performance.

For interest rate derivatives, the operations team reviews the daily exception report of EVE and NII limit breaches each business day and investigates every flagged item. Each exception must be resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report, and the team sends a list of aged items to management weekly for review. The control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for rate sensitivity limits. Evidence retained includes the daily exception report annotated with each item's disposition and date, the escalation records, and the weekly aged-item summaries sent to management.

Each month, management for the investment securities portfolio measures the EVE and NII limit breach indicator against its defined threshold as part of the enterprise indicator framework for rate sensitivity limits. When a breach occurs, management escalates it to the risk committee with a documented action plan and a named owner responsible for remediation. Evidence includes the monthly indicator results, the threshold comparison, and the escalation package with the action plan and owner assignment, all of which are retained to support review and follow-up in later months.

Each month, Treasury runs the rate shock analysis in Pellmark ALM and measures the results for every scenario against the limits approved by the Board. When a scenario exceeds its limit, Treasury escalates the breach to ALCO within five business days. It then brings the breach to the Board Risk Committee at that committee's next meeting, together with a remediation plan. Evidence of performance for the Treasury ALM function includes the monthly report with the limit comparison, the ALCO escalation notice with its date, and the Board Risk Committee meeting materials containing the remediation plan.

Treasury ALM grants access to the systems used to monitor and escalate EVE and NII limit breaches only through approved roles, and requests outside those roles are rejected before provisioning. Each quarter, the Treasury ALM manager recertifies all entitlements and documents any removals or role changes. Access for departing employees is revoked within one business day of separation. Evidence kept includes approved access requests, signed quarterly recertification reports and termination tickets with removal timestamps, all supporting compliance with the enterprise access standard for rate sensitivity limits.

The Treasury ALM process owner approves the written procedures that govern the response to EVE and NII limit breaches. The owner reviews them at least annually and publishes the current version to Treasury staff, with each approved version retained in the procedure library. Every review is evidenced by a record of the review date and the approver's name. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval kept with that record, which keeps practice in line with the enterprise policy on rate sensitivity limits that the procedures implement.

Each quarter, Treasury back-tests the deposit beta and prepayment speed assumptions in Pellmark ALM against actual results, and any variance above the approved tolerance is presented to ALCO with an explanation and proposed action. ALCO reviews and approves the full assumption set annually, and Model Risk performs an independent validation of the model every two years. Evidence retained includes the quarterly back-testing workpapers and variance reports, the ALCO minutes recording the presentation of exceptions and the annual assumption approval, and the biennial Model Risk validation report.
