The control also covers assumptions used for funds transfer pricing.

Each month, Treasury staff supporting Funds Transfer Pricing reconcile the balances and records that feed the ALM model assumptions back to the source system and document any differences. They also research reconciling items, and any item still open after 30 days is escalated for resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, consistent with the enterprise balancing standard for interest rate risk modeling. The signed reconciliation, the aging of open items and the escalation records are retained as evidence of performance.

Before any credit card underwriting file can be scheduled for closing, Halbrook Loan Origination automatically compares the recorded disclosure delivery dates against required waiting periods and tests the disclosed fees against tolerance limits. When either check fails, the system blocks scheduling and routes the exception to the closing manager, who corrects the disclosure or fee data and resubmits the file so the check runs again. The control runs on every file at the point of scheduling. Evidence consists of the system-generated validation results and exception queue history retained in Halbrook Loan Origination, showing each failed check, the closing manager's correction, and the passing result before the closing date was set.

Each month, the credit card underwriting supervisor reviews the disclosure timing report to confirm that required disclosures went to applicants within the expected window. Any exception above the established threshold is investigated, and the supervisor records the cause and the corrective action before signing off on the report. The signed report, investigation notes and documentation of follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for loan disclosures within the credit card underwriting function.

For each indirect auto lending application, Halbrook Loan Origination automatically compares disclosure delivery dates and fee amounts against required timing and tolerance limits before the loan can be scheduled for closing. A loan that fails either check is held from closing and routed to the closing manager's exception queue, where the closing manager corrects the disclosure or fee issue and resubmits the loan for validation. Halbrook Loan Origination keeps a system record of each check result, exception, correction and the closing manager's clearance, and that record serves as evidence the control was performed.

Each business day, the indirect auto lending operations team works the exception report that flags loans where disclosure timing fell outside requirements, reviewing every flagged item against the loan file. Each exception is resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report, and the reviewer records the disposition, the date and their initials on the worked report. Items that remain open past that window are aged and reported to management weekly. The annotated daily reports and the weekly aging summaries are retained as evidence that the control follows the enterprise escalation standard on loan disclosures.

This automated control in Halbrook Loan Origination applies to the mortgage servicing area and runs each time a loan is submitted for closing. Before the loan can be scheduled, the system compares recorded disclosure delivery dates against required waiting periods and tests fees against tolerance limits. Any loan that fails either check is blocked from scheduling and routed to the closing manager, who corrects the disclosure or fee issue and resubmits the file. The system retains the check results, exception routing history and resubmission timestamps in the loan record as evidence of operation.

Each business day, the mortgage servicing operations team works the daily exception report on disclosure timing and resolves or escalates every exception within two business days of its appearance on the report. Exceptions that remain open past that window are treated as aged items and reported to management weekly, with the item count and the reason each item is still open. The reviewer initials and dates the worked report and records the disposition of each exception. The annotated reports, escalation records and weekly aged-item summaries are retained as evidence that the control operates under the enterprise escalation standard for loan disclosures.

Loan servicing staff in the Equipment Leasing portfolio enter changes to loan terms in Corvessa Core Banking, and a second servicing reviewer independent of the preparer approves each change before it becomes effective. Each business day, servicing staff run a report of loans that were scheduled to reprice but did not reset. They research each exception and correct or resolve it within two business days. Retained evidence includes the reviewer approval recorded on each maintenance change and the daily exception report annotated with the disposition and resolution date for every item.

Each month, the equipment leasing supervisor reviews the report of escrow and rate resets processed during the period and confirms that the reset activity agrees with the underlying lease terms. Any exception above the established threshold is investigated with the responsible processor, and the supervisor documents the cause and the corrective action before signing the report to evidence completion of the review. The signed report, together with investigation notes and records of follow-up actions, is retained in the monthly control file for audit inspection. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard governing loan payment processing for the equipment leasing portfolio.

Each maintenance change to loan terms on home equity lending accounts in Corvessa Core Banking is entered by one servicing staff member and must be approved by a second reviewer before it takes effect. Every business day, servicing staff work through the system-generated rate reset exception report, which lists loans that were due to reprice but did not. Each exception is investigated and resolved within two business days of appearing on the report. The maker and checker approval trail for each term change is retained in Corvessa Core Banking, and the daily exception report is kept with resolution notes and completion dates recorded against each item.

The home equity lending process owner approves the written procedures covering escrow handling and rate resets, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to staff after each review. Each procedure document records the date of the latest review and the name of the approver, and the prior versions are retained for audit sampling. Any departure from the documented steps requires a written exception approval, which is kept with the procedure file. The procedure is mapped to the enterprise loan payment processing policy, and the review confirms that it remains aligned with that policy.

Each month, a Home Equity Lending operations analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used for escrow and rate resets against the source system. Reconciling items still open after 30 days are escalated, and a reviewer independent of the preparer signs off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days. The procedure applies the enterprise balancing standard to loan payment processing. The signed reconciliation workpaper, the aged reconciling-item listing, and the escalation correspondence are retained as evidence.

Within the loan booking and servicing function, every change to loan terms keyed in Corvessa Core Banking must be approved by a second reviewer before it takes effect. The reviewer compares the change to the source request and records approval in the system. Each business day, servicing staff work a system-generated report of loans that were due to reprice but did not. They research and correct or document every exception within two business days. The approved maintenance records, the daily exception reports with resolution notes, and the dates each item was closed are kept as evidence for Internal Audit testing.

The loan booking and servicing process owner approves the written procedures governing escrow analysis and interest rate resets, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to servicing staff after each review. Each review records the review date and the name of the approver, and this record is retained as evidence that the annual review took place. Any deviation from the procedures must have a documented exception approval before it is applied, and the approval is kept with the procedure records. The procedures carry out the enterprise policy on loan payment processing and are mapped to that policy so reviewers can trace each requirement to its source.

Each year, loan booking and servicing staff who handle escrow analyses and rate resets complete role-specific training that carries out the enterprise learning requirement for loan payment processing. The servicing manager tracks completion against the current roster of in-scope employees and, once the annual deadline passes, requests removal of process access for anyone still overdue, restoring it only after the training is finished. Evidence kept includes the annual completion report with the in-scope roster, the overdue list, and the access removal and reinstatement requests with dates for each affected employee.

Within the mortgage servicing function, any change to loan terms entered in Corvessa Core Banking is held until a second servicing staff member, independent of the person who keyed it, compares the change against the supporting documentation and approves it in the system. Each business day, servicing staff also run a report from Corvessa Core Banking that lists loans scheduled to reprice where the rate reset did not occur, and they research and correct every exception within two business days. Evidence retained includes the system approval trail showing maker and checker identities with timestamps, the daily exception report annotated with the cause, the corrective action, the resolution date and the reviewer's initials, and an aging log that shows each item was cleared within the two-business-day window.

The mortgage servicing process owner approves the written procedures covering escrow analysis and adjustable-rate resets, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to servicing staff. Each review records the review date and the approver. Any departure from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the procedure file. The procedures put into practice the enterprise policy on loan payment processing, and audit testing confirms that the version in use matches the approved, dated copy.

For small business loans in the sba lending portfolio, any change a loan servicing staff member enters to loan terms in Corvessa Core Banking must be approved by a second servicing reviewer before it posts. The reviewer checks the change against the supporting loan documents and records sign-off in the system. Each business day, servicing staff run an automated rate reset exception report that lists loans scheduled to reprice that did not. They research and correct every exception within two business days. The approved maintenance records and the daily exception reports, annotated with resolution notes and completion dates, are kept as evidence of performance.

The process owner for the government-guaranteed small business lending unit approves the written procedures covering escrow handling and interest rate resets, reviews them no less than once a year and publishes the current version to staff on the shared procedures site. Each review cycle records the review date and the name of the approver in the document's revision history, which is kept as the primary evidence of performance. Any departure from the approved procedures requires an exception approval that is documented and retained with the procedure file. These procedures put into practice the enterprise policy governing loan payment processing, and the approved document is mapped to that policy.

Each month, a loan servicing analyst in the small business administration lending unit reconciles the balances and supporting records for escrow and rate resets to the source system and documents every variance on a reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item that remains open beyond 30 days is escalated to the unit manager with an explanation and a target resolution date. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed worksheet and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed worksheet, the source system extract, and the escalation log are kept as evidence that the control follows the enterprise balancing standard for loan payment processing.

Each quarter, model owners attest in Rothmere Model Inventory that their model records are complete and accurate, covering models used in the BSA/AML program. Before any new or changed model goes into production, Model Risk performs an independent validation and records the results and any findings against the model's inventory entry. Findings stay open in Rothmere Model Inventory until Model Risk confirms remediation and closes them. Evidence kept includes the signed quarterly attestations, the validation reports with production approval, and the finding closure history.

Within the BSA/AML Program, each employee who takes part in setting or updating model validation status must finish role-specific training on model governance once a year. The BSA Officer reviews completion records every month. Any staff member who is past due has access to the model validation status process removed until the training is completed. Monthly completion reports, access removal and restoration tickets, and the annual training roster are kept as evidence, and together they show the enterprise learning requirement on model governance is being met.

Each quarter, model owners supporting card fraud operations attest that their entries in Rothmere Model Inventory are complete and accurate, including model purpose, ownership and current status. Before any new or changed model is used in production, Model Risk performs an independent validation and confirms that deployment is not approved until the validation is complete. Model Risk records validation findings, assigns owners and due dates, and monitors each finding until it is closed. Evidence retained includes the signed quarterly attestations, validation reports with production approval sign-off, and the findings log showing closure dates and supporting remediation documentation.

Each business day, the card fraud operations team reviews the exception report on model validation status and works every listed item. Each exception must be resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report. Any item still open past that window is treated as aged and goes to management in a weekly summary. The team keeps the daily report, its resolution or escalation notes, and the weekly aged-item summaries as evidence that the control meets the enterprise escalation standard for model governance.

The card fraud operations process owner approves the written procedures that govern model validation status, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to staff once each review is complete. Each review records the date and the name of the approver, and any deviation from the procedures may proceed only with a documented exception approval. The procedures carry out the enterprise model governance policy, and the approval records, review history and exception approvals are retained as evidence for audit testing.

Each quarter, owners of credit card underwriting models attest in Rothmere Model Inventory that their inventory records are complete and accurate, and the signed attestations are kept in the system as evidence. Before any new or changed credit card underwriting model goes into production use, Model Risk performs an independent validation, and deployment is held until that validation is complete. Model Risk records validation findings and follows each one to closure, keeping validation reports, finding logs and closure evidence for audit testing.

Each business day, the credit card underwriting operations team reviews the exception report on model validation status and either resolves or escalates every listed exception within two business days of its appearance. Items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged-item summary and presented to management on a weekly basis. The team keeps the annotated daily reports, escalation correspondence, and weekly aged-item summaries as evidence of performance. This control puts into practice the enterprise escalation standard for model governance.

For each new commercial card product or material change, the product owner prepares a risk assessment, obtains sign-off from Compliance, Operational Risk and Information Security, and submits the signed assessment to the New Product Committee before any launch activity proceeds. The committee reviews the assessment at its scheduled meeting and records its approval decision in the minutes, and the product may not launch until that approval is documented. Within six months of go-live, the product owner completes a post-implementation review and presents the results to the committee. The signed risk assessment, committee minutes showing approval, and the completed post-implementation review are retained in the committee's records as evidence of performance.

The process owner for commercial card approves the written procedures that govern launch approvals, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to staff. Each review records the review date and the approver's name. Any deviation from the procedures requires an exception approval, which is documented and retained with the procedure record. The procedures put into effect the enterprise policy on new product governance, and Internal Audit tests this linkage when it evaluates the control.

Employees in the online and mobile banking line of business who take part in launch approvals complete role-specific training once each year, as required by the enterprise learning requirement on new product governance. The business line's control owner tracks completion against the roster of approval participants and removes any overdue employee's access to the launch approval process until the training is finished. Evidence retained includes the annual completion report, the participant roster, and records showing access removal and restoration for overdue staff.

Before any contract with a critical or high-risk third party is signed, Procurement confirms that the third-party risk team has recorded a completed due diligence package covering security, financial and compliance reviews and has assigned the vendor a criticality rating. If any review is outstanding or no rating has been assigned, Procurement holds the contract and does not execute it until the third-party risk team closes the open items. This preventive check is performed for each in-scope contract within the contract management process, at the point of execution. Evidence retained includes the completed due diligence package with the assigned criticality rating and the record of Procurement's pre-signature confirmation, kept with the executed contract file for audit testing.

Each month, the contract management function compares the partner onboarding risk indicator against its defined threshold and records the result on the monthly indicator tracking report. When the indicator breaches the threshold, management escalates it to the risk committee with a documented action plan and an assigned owner, and records the escalation in the committee meeting materials and minutes. This control puts the enterprise indicator framework for fintech partnerships into practice. Retained evidence consists of the monthly tracking reports showing the indicator value and threshold, and, for any breach, the escalation memo, action plan, and evidence of owner assignment.

The contract management process owner approves the written partner onboarding procedures, which implement the enterprise policy on fintech partnerships, and reviews them at least annually. After each approval, the current version is published to staff so that onboarding activity follows the approved steps. Each version records its review date and approver, and the process owner keeps these records as evidence of the annual review. Any deviation from the procedures must have a documented exception approval, which is kept with the procedure records for audit testing.

Before any contract with a critical or high-risk third party is signed, Procurement confirms that the third-party risk team has recorded a completed due diligence package covering security, financial and compliance reviews, and has assigned the vendor a criticality rating. The hold applies to every such engagement, including arrangements that come through new product approval, and the contract stays unsigned until both conditions are documented. Procurement keeps the completed due diligence package, the assigned criticality rating and a dated sign-off showing the checks were confirmed before execution, and this record is retained with the contract file for audit sampling.

The process owner for new product approval approves the written partner onboarding procedures, which implement the enterprise policy on fintech partnerships, and publishes them to staff. The owner reviews the procedures at least annually and records the review date and approver on the document's version history each cycle. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, kept with the onboarding file for the affected partner. Evidence retained includes the approved and published procedure version, the annual review record showing date and approver, and the log of approved exceptions.

Each month, an analyst within the new product approval process reconciles the balances and records supporting fintech partner onboarding to the source system and documents any differences on the reconciliation workpaper. Any reconciling item that remains open beyond 30 days is escalated to management with its age, amount and planned resolution noted. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days after month end. The signed workpaper, the supporting source system extracts and the escalation records are retained as evidence that the enterprise balancing standard for fintech partnerships was applied.

The third-party risk management function grants access to systems that support partner onboarding only through approved roles, and each request is checked against the role catalog before it is provisioned. Each quarter, business owners recertify all onboarding entitlements, and the third-party risk management team keeps the signed recertification results along with records of any revocations. When a leaver is identified, access is removed within one business day, and the termination notice and the timestamped removal confirmation are retained as evidence. The control carries out the enterprise access standard as it applies to fintech partnerships.

Outbound email and file transfers originating from branch operations are automatically scanned for customer personal information, and any message or file that matches is blocked before it leaves the bank. Information Security reviews each blocked item within one business day to decide whether it should be released as a legitimate business transmission or held and escalated as a potential data loss event. The reviewer's decision, the date of review and the rationale for release or escalation are recorded in the blocked message review log, which Information Security retains as evidence of timely review.

Within branch operations, the employee who initiates an outbound data loss prevention action cannot be the one who approves it, and role design in the access model makes those two steps mutually exclusive. Each quarter, the branch operations control owner pulls a report of any users holding both the initiation and approval roles, reviews each conflict, and has the conflicting access removed. The signed quarterly report, the reviewer's notes on each conflict, and the access removal confirmations are retained as evidence of the review. This control puts into practice the enterprise separation-of-duties standard for protecting customer data.

Information Security reviews every outbound email and file transfer from brokerage operations that the data loss prevention scanning blocks for containing customer personal information. An analyst examines each blocked message within one business day of the block and either releases it with a documented business justification or confirms the block and escalates it for follow-up. The analyst records the disposition, review date, and reviewer for each message in the blocked-message review log, which Information Security keeps as evidence of timely review.

Each month, a supervisor in brokerage operations reviews the outbound data loss prevention report, investigating every exception that exceeds the defined threshold and noting the outcome. When the review is finished, the supervisor signs the report to attest that all above-threshold items were addressed. The signed report is retained together with investigation notes and records of any follow-up actions. This review is the unit's means of meeting the enterprise oversight standard for customer data protection.

Outbound email and file transfers originating from contact center operations are automatically scanned for customer personal information, and any message that matches a detection rule is blocked before it leaves the bank. Information Security reviews each blocked message within one business day of the block to decide whether it should be released, remains blocked, or is escalated as a potential data exposure. The reviewer records the decision and its rationale against each blocked item. The daily review log and the supporting block alerts are retained as evidence of timely review.

Each month, a contact center operations supervisor reviews the outbound data loss prevention report for the preceding period and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold, documenting the cause and any corrective action taken. When the review is complete, the supervisor signs the report to attest that all above-threshold exceptions were examined and resolved or escalated. The signed report, investigation notes and records of follow-up actions are retained as evidence of the review. This control carries out the requirements of the enterprise oversight standard on customer data protection.

Outbound email and file transfers leaving the bank are automatically scanned for customer personal information, and any message or file that matches the detection rules is blocked before delivery and routed to a review queue. Information Security analysts review each blocked item within one business day, deciding whether to release it as a legitimate business transmission or to keep it blocked and escalate it as a potential data exposure. The queue log is retained as evidence, recording each blocked item, the reviewing analyst, the time of review, the disposition and any escalation notes. The control sits within the data governance process area.

The data governance process owner approves the written procedures for outbound data loss prevention, which carry out the enterprise policy on customer data protection. The owner reviews them at least annually and publishes the approved version to staff on the internal procedures site. Each review is logged with the review date and the approver's name, and the prior version is kept for reference. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the review record as evidence.

Outbound email and file transfers originating from the online and mobile banking environment are automatically scanned for customer personal information, and any message or file that matches a detection rule is blocked before it leaves the bank. Information Security reviews each blocked item within one business day to decide whether it was a legitimate business transmission that can be released or a potential data exposure that must be escalated. The reviewer documents the disposition, the rationale, and the date of review in the blocked-message queue. Information Security retains the queue records and supporting screenshots as evidence of timely review for testing.

Each business day, the operations team supporting online and mobile banking reviews the outbound data loss prevention exception report and works every flagged item to resolution or escalation within two business days of the report date. Exceptions that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged-item summary and presented to management weekly for direction and follow-up. This control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for customer data protection as applied to the online and mobile banking channel. Evidence retained includes the daily exception report annotated with the disposition, reviewer and date for each item, along with the weekly aged-item summaries and records of their delivery to management.

Each month, a supervisor in online and mobile banking reviews the outbound data loss prevention report, investigates every exception above the defined threshold, and signs and dates the report to evidence completion of the review. Exception investigations are documented with the cause identified, the disposition reached, and any follow-up actions assigned, and these notes are kept with the signed report in the monthly control file for audit inspection. This review is the business line's means of implementing the enterprise oversight standard on customer data protection.

Within wealth client onboarding, each employee with a role in outbound data loss prevention completes role-specific training once per year, consistent with the enterprise learning requirement on customer data protection. The onboarding team manager reviews the training completion report monthly to identify staff whose annual training has lapsed. The manager arranges removal of process access for any overdue staff member and restores it only after the training record shows completion. The monthly completion reports, access removal and reinstatement requests, and individual training completion records are retained as evidence of performance.

Each business day, Payment Operations reconciles every payment suspense account supporting the loan booking and servicing process to the corresponding balance in Velistra General Ledger and investigates any open items. Unresolved items aged beyond 15 days go to the operations manager for follow-up, and those aged beyond 30 days are elevated to the Controller. No suspense item may be written off without the Controller's documented approval. The signed daily reconciliation, the aged-item listing with escalation notes, and write-off approvals are retained as evidence of performance.

Each month, a loan booking and servicing operations analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used for suspense account aging back to the source system, consistent with the enterprise balancing standard for payment suspense balances. Any reconciling item that has remained open for more than 30 days is escalated to servicing management for research and resolution, with the escalation noted on the reconciliation workpaper. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation, aging detail and escalation notes and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed reconciliation, aging report and escalation records are kept as evidence of performance.

Each month, the designated account owner within Deposit Operations reconciles every balance sheet account supporting escheatment and dormant accounts to the corresponding balance in Velistra General Ledger and documents the investigation and disposition of each reconciling item. Any reconciling item outstanding more than 30 days is escalated by the account owner for resolution, with the escalation noted on the reconciliation. An independent reviewer examines the completed reconciliation, including supporting detail and the status of aged items, and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed reconciliation, item aging detail and escalation records are retained as evidence of performance.

Each month, a supervisor in the escheatment and dormant accounts function reviews the reconciling item aging report and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold. Once the investigation is complete, the supervisor signs and dates the report to evidence the review. The signed report, along with documentation of each exception's investigation and any follow-up actions, is retained as evidence of control performance. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for clearing account balances.

Each month, Deposit Operations staff assigned to escheatment and dormant accounts reconcile the balances and supporting records used for reconciling item aging back to the source system and document any differences they find. Any reconciling item that has been open longer than 30 days is escalated for follow-up and resolution. Within ten business days of month end, a reviewer independent of the preparer examines the reconciliation, the aging schedule and the escalation notes and then signs off. The signed reconciliation, aging detail and escalation evidence are retained as support that the enterprise balancing standard for clearing account balances is being applied.

Each month, designated account owners within the retirement plan recordkeeping function reconcile every balance sheet account to Velistra General Ledger, researching and documenting any variance between subledger and general ledger balances. Reconciling items that remain open beyond 30 days are flagged on the aging schedule and escalated to management for resolution, with the cause and planned clearing date noted on the reconciliation. An independent reviewer examines each completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month-end. The signed reconciliation, supporting aging detail and escalation notes are retained as evidence of performance and review.

For retirement plan recordkeeping, Information Security grants system access used to age and clear reconciling items only through predefined roles that management has approved, and it retains the approved request and role mapping for each grant. Each quarter, the business owner recertifies all entitlements against current job duties, with signed recertification results and documented removals kept as evidence. When an employee leaves, access is revoked within one business day of the termination date, and the termination notice and removal timestamp are retained to show timely action. The control carries out the enterprise access standard as it applies to clearing account balances.

For each regulatory filing, regulatory reporting staff reconcile the report balances produced in Sorrelin Regulatory Reporting to the corresponding Velistra General Ledger balances, investigate any differences, and record every manual adjustment with its rationale and supporting documentation. Before the filing is submitted, a preparer independent of the reconciliation reviews the reconciliation and adjustments, and the Controller then signs off to approve submission. The completed reconciliation workpaper, the adjustment log with support, and the dated reviewer and Controller sign-offs are retained in the filing package as evidence of performance. This control falls within the general ledger and financial close process.

The process owner for General Ledger and Financial Close approves the written procedures for call report reconciliation and publishes them to staff once approved. The procedures are reviewed at least annually to confirm they still support the enterprise policy on regulatory filing accuracy. Each review is evidenced by the recorded review date and approver name on the procedure document, and the prior approved version is kept as well. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the reconciliation records for the affected filing period.

Before each filing, the regulatory reporting team reconciles report balances in Sorrelin Regulatory Reporting to Velistra General Ledger and investigates and resolves any differences. The preparer documents every manual adjustment with its supporting rationale. A reviewer independent of the preparer then checks the reconciliation and adjustments, and the Controller signs off before the filing is submitted. The signed reconciliation package, adjustment support, and dated reviewer and Controller approvals are kept with the filing records, and this control applies only to the regulatory reporting function.

Access to the systems used for call report reconciliation is provisioned only through approved roles, with each request reviewed against the role catalog before Information Security grants it. Each quarter, the regulatory reporting manager recertifies all entitlements. Any access that is inappropriate or no longer needed is flagged for removal, and the signed recertification and removal tickets are retained as evidence. Accounts belonging to leavers are disabled within one business day of the termination notice, and the deprovisioning log is kept to show timeliness, consistent with the enterprise access standard on regulatory filing accuracy.

The regulatory reporting process owner approves the written procedures for call report reconciliation, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to staff on the department's procedure site. Each review records the review date and the approver's name, and the approved version is kept as evidence alongside prior versions. Staff may deviate from the procedure only with a documented exception approval, which is filed with the reconciliation package for the affected quarter. The procedure carries out the enterprise policy on regulatory filing accuracy, and the annual review confirms that the two remain aligned.

Before each regulatory filing is submitted, the regulatory reporting team reconciles the report balances produced in Sorrelin Regulatory Reporting to the corresponding balances in Velistra General Ledger and investigates any variances. Each manual adjustment made to the filing is documented with its rationale and supporting calculation. A preparer independent of the reconciliation reviews the reconciliation and adjustments, and the Controller signs off before the filing is released. The signed reconciliation workpaper, adjustment support, reviewer evidence and Controller approval are retained with the filing package for each period, and the control covers regulatory reporting data.

The process owner for regulatory reporting data approves the written call report reconciliation procedures, reviews them at least once a year, and publishes the current version to the staff who perform the reconciliation. Each review leaves a record of the review date and the approver's name with the procedure document, and that record is kept as audit evidence. Staff may depart from the documented steps only with an exception approval that is documented and retained alongside the reconciliation file. The procedures carry out the enterprise policy on regulatory filing accuracy for this process.

Each month, a brokerage operations analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used for price verification back to the source system and documents any differences on the monthly reconciliation worksheet. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated to brokerage operations management, with the escalation date and owner noted on the worksheet. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed worksheet, the source system extract and the escalation log are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard for securities pricing.

Finance staff compare month-end security prices recorded in Ostrand Treasury Workstation against an independent second pricing source for every position in the investment securities portfolio, completing the comparison as part of the monthly close. Any price difference that exceeds the established tolerance is flagged as an exception and investigated to determine its cause before close is finalized. Treasury reviews each exception and records its challenge, including the price it accepts and the reasoning behind that decision. The retained evidence is the signed price comparison workbook, the exception log with investigation notes and Treasury's documented challenge for each item.

For the investment securities portfolio, the process owner approves the written price verification procedures, which implement the enterprise securities pricing policy, and publishes the approved version to the staff who perform price verification. The process owner reviews the procedures at least annually, and each review's date and approver are recorded on the procedure document as evidence. Any deviation from the procedures requires a documented exception approval, and that approval is retained with the procedure records for audit inspection.

Each quarter the tax team prepares the income tax provision for the personal trust administration business and reconciles the provision to the returns as filed, investigating and documenting any return-to-provision differences. The Controller reviews the provision calculation and the reconciliation and evidences approval by sign-off before the quarterly close is finalized. Filing deadlines are tracked on a compliance calendar that the tax team maintains. The signed provision workpapers, the reconciliation with explanations of variances, and the calendar are retained as evidence of performance.

Brokerage operations staff record each trade or contribution error in the error log within Ivelle Wealth Platform when it is identified, noting the account, error type, cause and estimated client impact. The responsible staff member processes the correction within one business day of identification and updates the log entry with the correcting transaction reference and completion date. Before any make-whole payment is released to a client, an operations supervisor reviews the calculation and supporting trade detail and records approval in the log. The completed log, correction records and supervisor approvals are retained as evidence of performance.

Each month, a brokerage operations supervisor reviews the report of trade error corrections processed during the prior period and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold to confirm the correction was appropriate and properly supported. Once the review and any required follow-up are complete, the supervisor signs and dates the report to evidence sign-off. The signed report, investigation notes and documentation of any remediation actions are retained as evidence of review. This control implements the enterprise oversight standard on client trade processing.

Wealth operations staff record each trade or contribution error affecting portfolio management accounts in the error log within Ivelle Wealth Platform at the time the error is identified, noting the account, error type, root cause and calculated client impact. The error is corrected within one business day of identification. Where the client is owed a make-whole payment, an operations supervisor reviews the calculation and approves the payment before it is released. The completed log entry, the correcting transaction and the supervisor's documented approval of any make-whole payment are retained in Ivelle Wealth Platform as evidence of performance.

Each month, portfolio management staff reconcile the balances and supporting records for trade error corrections against the source system and document any differences on a reconciliation worksheet. Reconciling items that remain open beyond 30 days are escalated, with the escalation date and the item's aging recorded on the worksheet. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month-end. The signed worksheet, source system extracts and escalation records are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise balancing standard for client trade processing.

Within the retirement plan recordkeeping function, operations staff record each trade or contribution error in the error log maintained in Ivelle Wealth Platform at the time the error is identified, noting the affected plan, participant account, error type and root cause. Staff process the correcting entry no later than one business day after the error is logged and update the log entry with the correction date and reference. Where a client make-whole payment is needed, an operations supervisor reviews the gain or loss calculation and approves the payment before release. Evidence retained includes the completed error log entries, correction transaction records and the supervisor's documented approval of each make-whole payment.

Access to the systems used for trade error corrections in retirement plan recordkeeping is provisioned by Information Security only through approved roles, and each request must carry documented manager approval before an entitlement is assigned. Each quarter, the retirement plan recordkeeping operations manager recertifies all user entitlements tied to trade error corrections, and Information Security removes or adjusts any access flagged as inappropriate. When an employee leaves, Information Security revokes that person's access within one business day of the termination notice. Signed quarterly recertification reports, access request tickets with approvals, and termination removal logs showing timestamps are retained as evidence that the control meets the enterprise access standard for client trade processing.

Within retirement plan recordkeeping, trade error corrections must be initiated by one employee and approved by a different employee, and role design prevents a single user from completing both steps. Each quarter, the recordkeeping operations manager reviews a report of users assigned both the initiation and approval roles, has any conflicting access removed, and documents the outcome. The signed report, removal requests, and confirmation that access was revoked are retained as evidence. This control applies the enterprise SoD standard to client trade processing.

Manual account adjustments greater than $1,000 keyed into Corvessa Core Banking by branch operations staff are placed in a pending status and do not post until a second authorized user reviews and approves them, and system role settings prevent the user who entered an adjustment from also approving it. Each business day, Deposit Operations reviews the report of the prior day's approved adjustments to confirm that every item over the threshold carries a separate approver and is supported by documentation. The reviewer signs off on the daily report and retains it with any follow-up notes on exceptions, and the system's pending-item and approval history remains available as evidence of the dual-control enforcement.

The branch operations manager confirms each year that every employee who performs or approves manual adjustments has completed the role-specific training required under the enterprise learning requirement for manual account postings. Completion status is tracked throughout the year. When an employee becomes overdue, the manager has that employee's access to the manual adjustment process removed and restores it only after the training is complete. Evidence retained for review includes the annual completion report, the overdue listing, and the related access removal and reinstatement records.

Manual account adjustments greater than $1,000 keyed into Corvessa Core Banking by Deposit Account Servicing staff are placed in a pending status and do not post until a second user with approval authority releases them. A system-enforced restriction blocks the user who entered an adjustment from also approving it. Each business day, Deposit Operations reviews the daily report of approved adjustments to confirm that entries are supported and appropriately authorized, and it follows up on any exceptions. The signed or initialed daily report, together with the system approval history for each adjustment, is retained as evidence of performance.

Each month, deposit account servicing management compares the volume of manual adjustments posted to customer accounts against the defined threshold for this risk indicator, as required by the enterprise indicator framework for manual account postings. Any breach of the threshold is escalated to the risk committee with a documented action plan and a named owner responsible for remediation. The monthly indicator results, threshold comparisons, escalation submissions, and the related committee minutes and action plans are retained as evidence of performance.

Manual account adjustments above $1,000 entered in Corvessa Core Banking for the loan booking and servicing process are held in a pending status until a second user approves them. A system-enforced restriction prevents the entering user from approving their own adjustment. Each business day, Deposit Operations reviews the daily report of approved adjustments to confirm that each one carries separate entry and approval user IDs and has adequate support. Reviewers sign off on the report and retain it with any follow-up notes as evidence of performance.

The loan booking and servicing process owner approves the written procedures governing manual adjustments, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to staff so that those performing adjustments work from the approved text. Each review records the review date and the name of the approver, and any deviation from the procedures may proceed only with a documented exception approval kept with the procedure file. The procedures implement the enterprise policy on manual account postings, and the approved procedure, review record and exception approvals serve as the evidence retained for testing.

Each month, an analyst in Loan Booking & Servicing reconciles the balances and supporting records for manual adjustments back to the source system, investigating and documenting any differences identified. Reconciling items that remain open beyond 30 days are escalated, and an independent reviewer evidences sign-off on the completed reconciliation within ten business days of month end. The signed reconciliation, aged reconciling item listing, and escalation records are retained as evidence, and the procedure operates as the business line's implementation of the enterprise balancing standard for manual account postings.

Each month, Compliance runs a query in Ylvara Data Warehouse to identify newly opened accounts that have shown no activity 60 days after opening, scoped to accounts originated through branch operations. For every account on the resulting report, the Compliance reviewer locates and confirms the customer consent evidence supporting the account opening and records the outcome on the monthly worksheet. Any account lacking adequate consent evidence is logged as an exception and referred to human resources for review of the associated employee conduct. The query parameters, the population report, the completed review worksheet with reviewer sign-off and date, and the exception referrals to human resources are retained as evidence of performance.

Each business day, the branch operations team works the daily exception report that flags accounts lacking consent evidence, and every exception is either resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report. Items that age past that window are compiled and reported to branch operations management on a weekly basis for review and direction. The team retains the worked daily reports, annotated with the resolution or escalation taken and the date of action, along with the weekly aged-item reports sent to management, as evidence of performance. This procedure carries out the enterprise escalation standard on sales practices.

Each month, Compliance extracts from Ylvara Data Warehouse a listing of newly opened accounts that show no customer activity 60 days after opening, limited to accounts originated through the online and mobile banking channel. For each account on the listing, the Compliance reviewer confirms that documented evidence of customer consent exists and agrees to the account record, noting any account where consent evidence is missing or inconsistent as an exception. Exceptions are referred to human resources for review of the employees associated with the account opening. The monthly extract, the reviewer's completed testing worksheet with sign-off and date, and the exception referral are retained as control evidence.

Each year, every online and mobile banking employee with a role in capturing or maintaining account consent evidence must complete role-specific training, which carries out the enterprise learning requirement on sales practices. The business line manager tracks completion status against the assigned population and removes process access for anyone past the annual due date, restoring it only after the training is finished. Retained evidence includes the completion records, the overdue listings with dates of access removal, and the corresponding reinstatement records.

For commercial loan origination, Halbrook Loan Origination automatically checks each approver's delegated lending authority against the approval matrix and blocks booking until the loan amount and risk grade fall within that approver's limit. Any override of this check is routed to Credit Administration, which reviews the full override log once a week to confirm that each override has proper approval. Items without approval are escalated to the Chief Credit Officer for resolution. Credit Administration keeps the weekly override log with the reviewer's sign-off and date and the escalation notes for each unapproved item as evidence of performance.

The commercial loan origination process owner approves the written procedures governing loan approval limits and reviews them at least once a year, then publishes the current version to staff. Each review is logged with the review date and the name of the approver, and the approved procedure document and review log are retained as evidence. Any deviation from the documented limits is permitted only with a written exception approval, which is kept with the loan file. These procedures put into practice the enterprise policy on credit approval authority.

For commercial real estate lending, Halbrook Loan Origination automatically checks the approving officer's delegated lending authority against the configured approval matrix and blocks booking of any loan that exceeds that authority. Any override of this hard stop is routed to Credit Administration, where an analyst reviews the system-generated override log each week to confirm that every override carries documented approval at the required level. Overrides lacking proper approval are escalated to the Chief Credit Officer for resolution. The weekly override log, signed off by the reviewer, is retained with the related escalation correspondence and resolution notes as evidence of performance.

On a monthly basis, a supervisor in commercial real estate lending reviews the loan approval limits report to confirm that each approved credit fell within the approving officer's delegated authority. Any exception above the established threshold is investigated with the responsible lender, and the supervisor signs the report to evidence completion of the review. The signed report, together with documentation of exception research and any resulting follow-up actions, is retained as evidence of performance. This control operates under the enterprise oversight standard governing credit approval authority.

The commercial real estate lending process owner approves the written procedures that set loan approval limits, reviews them at least annually, and publishes the current version to lending staff once approved. Each review records the review date and the name of the approver on the procedure document, and those records are kept as evidence of performance. Any deviation from the stated limits requires a documented exception approval, which is retained with the related credit file. The procedure implements the enterprise policy on credit approval authority, and the annual review confirms that the limits still align with that policy.

Before any loan is booked in Halbrook Loan Origination, the system checks the approver's delegated lending authority against the configured approval matrix and blocks booking when the authority is insufficient. Any override of that check is routed to Credit Administration. Credit Administration reviews the system-generated override log each week and confirms that every override has a documented approval. Items found without approval are escalated to the Chief Credit Officer. The control covers Middle Market Lending, and evidence retained consists of the weekly override log with reviewer sign-off and the escalation records sent to the Chief Credit Officer.

The process owner for middle market lending approves the written procedures governing loan approval limits, reviews them at least annually against the enterprise policy on credit approval authority that they implement, and publishes the current version to staff. Each review records the review date and the name of the approver in the procedure's version history, which is retained as evidence of the annual review and approval. Any deviation from the stated approval limits requires a documented exception approval, kept with the related credit file and available for audit testing.

For Middle Market Lending, role design prevents the same employee from both initiating and approving a change to loan approval limits, so the maker and checker steps always sit with different people. Each quarter, a report of users who hold both the initiation and approval roles is reviewed, and any conflicting access found is removed. The reviewed report and the record of removed conflicts are retained as evidence. This procedure puts the enterprise separation-of-duties standard on credit approval authority into practice for the segment.

For loans secured under the collateral management process, the valuation unit orders each third-party appraisal from the approved appraiser panel and, before the loan closes, completes a review checklist that tests the comparable sales used, confirms the appraiser's independence from the lending decision, and assesses whether the concluded value is adequately supported. Where a valuation is more than 120 days old at the time of review, the unit re-orders a new appraisal rather than relying on the existing report. The reviewer signs and dates the completed checklist, which is retained in the loan file with the appraisal order confirmation and any re-order request as evidence that the control was performed.

Each month, a collateral management supervisor reviews the appraisal review report and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold, documenting the cause and the resolution or remediation steps taken. Once the review is complete, the supervisor signs and dates the report to evidence the review. The signed report, together with exception notes and records of any follow-up actions, is retained so that it is available for testing. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for collateral valuation.

Each month, a collateral management analyst reconciles the balances and records that support appraisal review to the source system and investigates any differences. Any reconciling item that remains open beyond 30 days is escalated to collateral management leadership with an explanation and a target resolution date. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days, as the enterprise balancing standard on collateral valuation requires. The signed reconciliation, the supporting item aging and the escalation correspondence are retained as evidence of performance.

For commercial loan origination, the valuation unit orders each third-party appraisal from the approved appraiser panel and, before the loan closes, reviews the completed report against a standard review checklist covering the comparable sales used, the appraiser's independence from the borrower and lending staff, and whether the concluded value is adequately supported. Any valuation with an effective date more than 120 days old at the time of review is not accepted, and the unit re-orders a new appraisal from the panel. The reviewer signs and dates the completed checklist, which is retained in the loan file with the appraisal report and the order record as evidence that the review was performed before closing.

Each month, a Commercial Loan Origination supervisor reviews the appraisal review report for the prior period. The supervisor looks into every exception that exceeds the defined threshold, documents the cause and the resolution, and signs the report to confirm the review is complete. The signed report, together with the exception investigation notes and any follow-up actions, is retained as evidence. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard on collateral valuation at the business-line level.

Within commercial loan origination, the employee who initiates an appraisal review cannot also approve it, and role design blocks a single user from completing both steps. Each quarter, Credit Administration pulls a report of users who hold both the initiator and approver roles, reviews every match, and has conflicting access removed or reassigned before signing off. The signed report, notes on how each conflict was resolved, and the access change tickets are retained as evidence. This control puts the enterprise separation-of-duties standard into effect for collateral valuation.

For each construction loan, the valuation unit places the appraisal order only with a firm on the approved panel. Before the loan closes, a reviewer completes the review checklist, which assesses the comparable sales used, confirms the appraiser's independence, and evaluates whether the concluded value is adequately supported. If an appraisal effective date is more than 120 days old at the time of review, the unit orders a new valuation rather than relying on the existing report. The signed checklist, the panel order record and any re-order documentation are retained in the loan file as evidence of performance for Construction Lending.

Each month, a Construction Lending supervisor reviews the appraisal review report and checks the completed appraisal reviews for the period against expected volumes and turnaround. Any exception above the defined threshold is investigated with the responsible reviewer, and the supervisor records the cause and the corrective action taken before signing the report as evidence of review. The signed report, exception notes and documentation of follow-up actions are retained with the monthly control file. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard on collateral valuation for the construction lending portfolio.

For consumer mortgage lending, the valuation unit orders each third-party appraisal from the approved appraiser panel. Before the loan closes, a valuation unit reviewer completes the standard review checklist, which documents the adequacy of comparable sales, confirms appraiser independence and assesses whether the reported value is adequately supported. Any valuation more than 120 days old at the time of review is re-ordered rather than relied upon. The signed checklist and the appraisal order record from the approved panel are kept in the loan file as evidence of review.

Each business day, the consumer mortgage lending operations team reviews the daily appraisal review exception report and works every listed exception to resolution or escalation within two business days. Any item still open past that window is classified as aged and goes to management in a weekly aged-exception summary. The operations team keeps the annotated daily report, with the disposition, reviewer initials and date for each exception, along with the weekly summaries sent to management, as evidence of performance. This control applies the enterprise escalation standard for collateral valuation to the consumer mortgage lending appraisal review process.

For home equity lending, the valuation unit places each third-party appraisal order with a firm from the approved appraiser panel. Before the loan closes, a valuation reviewer completes the review checklist, assessing the comparable sales used, the appraiser's independence from the transaction and whether the report adequately supports the concluded value. Any valuation dated more than 120 days before closing is not accepted and a new appraisal is ordered. The signed and dated checklist, the appraisal report and any re-order request are retained in the loan file as evidence of review.

Each month, a designated analyst in the home equity lending unit reconciles the balances and records that support appraisal review against the source system and documents each variance on the reconciliation workpaper. Any reconciling item that remains open for more than 30 days is escalated to the unit manager, and the escalation is noted with its age and planned resolution. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days of month end. The signed workpaper, source system extract and escalation log are retained as evidence that the enterprise balancing standard for collateral valuation is being applied.

In Home Equity Lending, appraisal review is split between two employees: one initiates the review and a different employee approves it, and role design prevents a single user from completing both steps. Each quarter, a report listing users who hold both the initiation and approval roles is reviewed, and any conflicting access found is removed. This applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to collateral valuation. The quarterly conflict report, the reviewer's sign-off, and records of each access removal are retained as evidence of performance.

Before a clear-to-close can be issued on any consumer installment loan, the assigned underwriter works through the income verification checklist in Halbrook Loan Origination and marks each required document as received. A system hard stop holds the file until every checklist item is satisfied or the underwriting manager approves an exception, and the manager's approval and stated rationale are logged against the loan record. Each week a report of open exceptions is generated and reviewed so that outstanding items are followed up. The completed checklist, the exception approvals and the weekly open exception reports are kept as evidence that the control operated.

Each business day, the consumer installment lending operations team reviews the daily exception report for loans with missing or deficient borrower income documentation, and every exception is resolved or escalated within two business days of appearing on the report. Items that remain open beyond that window are compiled into an aged exception summary and presented to management each week for review and direction. The team retains the annotated daily report, a log of resolution or escalation actions with dates and reviewer initials, and the weekly aged summary with evidence of management review. The procedure puts into practice the enterprise escalation standard on borrower income verification.

In Consumer Installment Lending, the initiation and the approval of borrower income documentation are assigned to separate employees, and role design enforces this so that no single user can both input and approve income verification. Each quarter, a report listing users who hold both the initiator and approver roles is generated and reviewed. Any conflicting access identified in the review is removed, and the reviewed report and the record of each removal are retained as evidence. The control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to borrower income verification.

Within Consumer Mortgage Lending, the assigned underwriter works through the income verification checklist in Halbrook Loan Origination for every file before closing. Each checklist item has to be marked received, or else carry an exception approved by the underwriting manager, before the system will allow a clear-to-close to be issued. Every week, open exceptions are pulled into a report for follow-up. The completed checklists, the manager exception approvals and the weekly open exception reports are kept in Halbrook Loan Origination as evidence that the control operated.

The Consumer Mortgage Lending operations team reviews the daily exception report for income documentation each business day and works each flagged item to confirm that borrower income verification meets the enterprise escalation standard. Every exception must be resolved, or escalated to the responsible supervisor, within two business days of appearing on the report. Each week, items that are aged past that window are summarized and presented to management for review and direction. Evidence retained includes the daily exception report annotated with the resolution or escalation date for each item, along with the weekly aged-item summary provided to management.

On a monthly basis, the credit card underwriting supervisor reviews the income documentation report, investigates each exception that exceeds the established threshold, and records the resolution or follow-up required. Once the review is complete, the supervisor signs the report to attest that all threshold exceptions were examined. The signed report, exception notes, and records of any follow-up actions are retained as evidence of performance. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard governing verification of borrower income.

For each home equity lending application, the assigned underwriter completes the income verification checklist in Halbrook Loan Origination and marks each required document as received before the file moves to closing. A system hard stop prevents a clear-to-close from being issued while any checklist item is outstanding, unless the underwriting manager has approved an exception in the system with a documented rationale. Each week, open exceptions are compiled into a report and distributed for follow-up so that aged items are pursued to resolution. Evidence retained includes the completed checklist and item-level receipt status in the loan file, the manager's exception approval record with date and rationale, and copies of the weekly open exception reports.

Each business day, the home equity lending operations team works the daily exception report for income documentation and either resolves or escalates every listed exception within two business days of its appearance on the report. Items not cleared within that window are treated as aged and presented to management in a weekly summary showing exception age, the status of the borrower income verification and the assigned owner. The team keeps the annotated daily reports, escalation records and weekly aged-item summaries as evidence that the control operated. The control carries out the enterprise escalation standard for borrower income verification within home equity lending.

For each indirect auto lending application, the assigned underwriter completes the income verification checklist in Halbrook Loan Origination before the loan proceeds to closing. The system blocks issuance of a clear-to-close until every checklist item is marked received or the underwriting manager approves an exception, and that approval is logged in the loan file with the approver's user ID and timestamp. Each week, a report of open exceptions is generated and retained with evidence of the underwriting manager's review and follow-up on aged items. The completed checklists, exception approvals, and weekly reports are kept in Halbrook Loan Origination as audit evidence.

In Indirect Auto Lending, one employee initiates income documentation for borrower income verification and a different employee approves it. Role design enforces this split so that no single user can both create and approve the same record, consistent with the enterprise separation-of-duties standard. Each quarter, a report of users who hold both the initiation and approval roles is generated and reviewed, and any conflicting access found is removed. The quarterly report, the reviewer's sign-off and evidence of each role removal are retained as support for the control.

Before any contract is signed, the third-party risk team assigns each card production and fulfillment vendor a criticality rating and obtains the vendor's SOC reports and a review of its financial condition. Vendors rated critical are reassessed annually, with refreshed SOC reports and financial reviews collected at each cycle. Criticality ratings, due diligence documents and reassessment dates are recorded in Draycott Contract Repository, which serves as evidence of completion and tracks reviews coming due.

Each month, a supervisor in the card production and fulfillment function reviews the report on vendor due diligence packages and examines every exception that exceeds the established threshold. The supervisor works each such exception to resolution or documents the follow-up required, then signs the report to show the review is complete. The signed report, along with notes on the investigation and any follow-up actions taken, is retained as evidence. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard governing the onboarding of critical vendors.

Before any contract supporting the online and mobile banking channel is signed, the third-party risk team assigns the vendor a criticality rating and obtains its SOC reports and a financial review. Vendors rated critical are reassessed by the same team every year. The criticality rating, SOC reports, financial review results, and the dates of each annual reassessment are stored and tracked in Draycott Contract Repository, which serves as audit evidence that due diligence was finished before execution and that reassessments were completed on schedule.

The process owner for online and mobile banking approves the written procedures governing vendor due diligence packages, which carry out the enterprise policy on critical vendor onboarding, and publishes the approved version to staff. These procedures are reviewed no less than annually, and each review is logged with the review date and the name of the approver so the evidence can be retrieved at audit. Any departure from the procedures is allowed only with a documented exception approval, which is retained with the procedure records.

Within the third-party risk management process, the third-party risk team assigns a criticality rating to every vendor at onboarding and, before any contract is signed, obtains and reviews the vendor's SOC reports and a financial review appropriate to that rating. Vendors rated critical are reassessed annually, with the team refreshing the SOC report and financial review and confirming that the criticality rating still holds. The criticality rating, the SOC reports and financial reviews collected, reviewer sign-off and the date of each annual reassessment are recorded and tracked in Draycott Contract Repository, which serves as the evidence of performance.

Each month, third-party risk management staff calculate the risk indicator for vendor due diligence packages and compare the result to the defined threshold set for critical vendor onboarding under the enterprise indicator framework. When the indicator breaches the threshold, the third-party risk management lead escalates it to the risk committee with a documented action plan and a named owner responsible for remediation. Evidence retained includes the monthly indicator calculation and threshold comparison, the escalation memo to the risk committee, and the committee minutes recording the action plan, owner and target completion date.

Within the third-party risk management function, role design ensures that the employee who initiates a vendor due diligence package cannot also approve it, so initiation and approval for critical vendor onboarding always rest with two different people. Each quarter, the function generates a report of all users assigned both the initiator and approver roles, reviews every flagged user, and has conflicting access removed. The reviewer signs and dates the quarterly report and retains it with evidence of each role removal for audit inspection. This control puts the enterprise SoD standard into practice for the onboarding of critical vendors.

For retirement plan recordkeeping, the business owner of each critical vendor reviews that vendor's service level report in Draycott Contract Repository every quarter and records any service level breach identified during the review. The business owner also keeps a current exit plan for each vendor that supports a critical service and confirms the plan has been tested. Evidence retained in Draycott Contract Repository includes the quarterly service level reports with the reviewer's sign-off and review date, the breach log entries, and the exit plan with documentation of its most recent test.

Each month, the retirement plan recordkeeping supervisor reviews the report of vendor service level agreement breaches for the prior period and investigates every exception that exceeds the established threshold, documenting the cause and any corrective action agreed with the vendor. On completing the review, the supervisor signs and dates the report as evidence that it was performed. The signed report, investigation notes and records of follow-up actions are retained in the unit's control evidence files for testing. This control puts into practice the enterprise oversight standard on vendor service levels.

Each month, third-party risk management staff compile the count of vendor service level agreement breaches and compare the result to the defined threshold set for this indicator under the enterprise indicator framework. When the indicator exceeds that threshold, management escalates the breach to the risk committee together with a remediation action plan that names an accountable owner and a target date. The monthly indicator calculation, the threshold comparison, the escalation package and the committee minutes recording review of the action plan are retained as evidence of performance.

For the data center and cloud hosting environment, Information Security runs Kestrin Vulnerability Scanner against all inventoried assets every week and reviews the results once each scan cycle completes.
