Each critical finding opens a remediation ticket in Orveth Change Manager with a 30-day deadline, and the ticket stays open until a follow-up scan confirms the fix. Any critical finding that cannot be remediated within the deadline requires a documented exception approved by Information Security. Evidence retained includes the weekly scan output, the Orveth Change Manager tickets with their open and close dates, and the signed exception approvals.

The process owner for Data Center & Cloud Hosting maintains written procedures that set patch deadlines and carry out the enterprise policy on vulnerability remediation. The owner approves the procedures, reviews them at least once a year and publishes the current version to staff. Each review records the review date and the approver's identity. Any departure from the procedure is allowed only with a documented exception approval, which is kept with the procedure record as evidence.

Within data center and cloud hosting, the employee who initiates a patch deadline cannot be the employee who approves it, and this separation is enforced through role design that keeps the initiator and approver roles distinct. Each quarter, the platform manager reviews a report of all users who hold both roles and removes every conflicting access assignment found. The reviewed report, annotated with the disposition of each conflict and the date of removal, is retained as evidence of performance. The control implements the enterprise separation-of-duties standard as it applies to vulnerability remediation.

Each week, Kestrin Vulnerability Scanner runs an automated scan across every asset recorded in the inventory for the IT operations and resilience area, and IT staff review the results once the scan completes. For any finding rated critical, a remediation ticket is raised in Orveth Change Manager with a due date set 30 days out, and progress is tracked against that deadline until closure. Where a critical finding cannot be fixed within the window, the asset owner submits an exception request that must be approved by Information Security before the deadline passes. Retained evidence includes the weekly scan reports, the Orveth Change Manager ticket history showing open and close dates, and the signed Information Security exception approvals.

Each business day, the IT operations team works the exception report listing servers and endpoints that have missed or are at risk of missing their patch deadlines, in line with the enterprise escalation standard for vulnerability remediation. Within two business days of an exception first appearing, the assigned analyst either resolves it and records the remediation date or escalates it to the asset owner, noting the reason and the expected fix date on the report. Once a week, items that remain open past that window are compiled into an aged-exceptions summary and sent to IT operations and resilience management for review. The annotated daily reports, escalation emails and weekly summaries with management sign-off are retained on the team's shared drive as evidence of performance.

Each week, Kestrin Vulnerability Scanner runs an automated scan against every asset recorded in the inventory as part of the bank's vulnerability management process. Any finding rated critical automatically generates a ticket in Orveth Change Manager with a remediation due date 30 days out, and the asset owner must close the ticket by that date or obtain an exception. No exception is valid unless Information Security has approved it. Evidence retained includes the weekly scan output, the Orveth Change Manager ticket history showing open and close dates against the 30-day deadline, and the documented Information Security approval for each exception granted.

The vulnerability management process owner approves the written procedures that set patch remediation deadlines and reviews them at least once a year to confirm they still carry out the enterprise policy on vulnerability remediation. After each approval, the process owner publishes the current version to staff so that teams applying patches work from the approved deadlines. Each version records the review date and the approver's name, and prior versions are kept as evidence of the annual review. Any deviation from the stated deadlines needs an exception approval documented and retained with the procedure records before the deviation is allowed.

Within commercial deposit services, operations staff perform an independent verbal confirmation with the customer before releasing any outgoing wire over $25,000 or any wire to a beneficiary not previously used. The operator places the call to the telephone number on file in Corvessa Core Banking, never to a number supplied on the wire request itself, and logs the call outcome, number dialed, and customer contact in Brisance Wire Manager. A second operator must review and approve that callback record in Brisance Wire Manager before the system permits release. Evidence retained consists of the callback entry and the second operator's approval within Brisance Wire Manager for each qualifying wire.

Within commercial deposit services, outgoing wire transfers must be initiated by one employee and approved for release by a different employee, and role design prevents a single user from completing both steps. Each quarter, the commercial deposit services manager reviews a report listing any users who hold both the initiation and approval roles and has every conflicting access removed. The reviewed report is retained as evidence, signed and dated, with removal confirmations attached. The control applies the enterprise separation-of-duties standard to outgoing wire release.

For each outgoing wire over $25,000, and for any wire to a beneficiary not previously paid, operations staff call the customer at the telephone number on file in Corvessa Core Banking. They never use the number supplied on the wire request. The operator documents the callback in Brisance Wire Manager, including the number dialed, the date and time, and the outcome, and a second operator must review and approve that callback record before the system allows the wire to be released. This control covers wires originated through foreign exchange services, and the approved callback entries retained in Brisance Wire Manager serve as evidence of performance.

Each month, a Foreign Exchange Services supervisor reviews the wire release report covering outgoing wire transfers released during the period, looking for any items that fall outside expected parameters. Exceptions above the defined threshold are investigated with the releasing staff, and the supervisor records the outcome and any corrective action before signing and dating the report. The signed report, supporting investigation notes and documentation of follow-up actions are retained as evidence. This control puts the enterprise oversight standard for outgoing wire transfers into practice at the business unit level.

Before releasing any outgoing wire over $25,000, or any wire to a beneficiary not previously paid, Payment Operations staff call the customer at the telephone number on file in Corvessa Core Banking rather than any number supplied with the request. The operator logs the callback in Brisance Wire Manager, including the number dialed, the person reached, and the confirmation obtained. A second operator must review and approve that callback record before the wire can be released, and the approved record is retained in Brisance Wire Manager as evidence. The same callback and dual-approval requirement covers real-time payments.

Each month, a real-time payments supervisor reviews the wire release report for the prior period and investigates every exception above the established threshold, documenting the cause and resolution for each item. After completing the review, the supervisor signs the report to attest that all exceptions have been addressed or escalated as needed. The signed report, investigation notes, and records of any follow-up actions are retained as evidence of performance. This control carries out the enterprise oversight standard for outgoing wire transfers.

For outgoing wire transfers processed through real-time payments, system role design ensures that initiation and approval of a wire release are completed by two different employees, so no single user can both enter and release a payment. Each quarter, Payment Operations management runs a report of all users assigned both the initiator and approver roles, reviews each conflict, and has the conflicting access removed. The reviewer retains the signed and dated quarterly report, together with evidence that each flagged role was removed, as support that the enterprise separation-of-duties standard is applied to outgoing wires.

Each month, a wire transfer operations analyst reconciles the balances and supporting records used for wire release back to the source system, in line with the enterprise balancing standard for outgoing wire transfers. Any reconciling item still open after 30 days is escalated to wire transfer operations management, with the escalation date and status recorded on the reconciliation. A reviewer independent of the preparer examines the completed reconciliation and signs off within ten business days after month end. The signed reconciliation, source system extracts, aging of open items and escalation records are kept in the monthly reconciliation file as evidence of performance.

Second-line testing found that three generic administrator accounts on Velistra General Ledger were held outside the privileged access vault, which left their credentials directly available to support staff without check-out or rotation. Session logs for these accounts were also not reviewed for four months. During that period, administrative activity on the ledger was not independently monitored.

Compliance monitoring showed that fourteen user accounts in Velistra General Ledger had been set up directly by system administrators rather than routed through the required approval workflow. No documented approval exists for these accounts. The provisioning control therefore did not operate as designed for this population.

Independent risk testing found that exposure limits had gone more than two years without review for 7 of the 20 ACH originators sampled. For these originators, no evidence was available that limits had been reassessed against current financial condition or origination volumes. As a result, the limits in place may no longer reflect the credit and settlement risk each originator presents.

The risk review concluded that two qualitative adjustments applied to the credit loss reserve, together amounting to $14 million, were recorded without any documented rationale supporting their basis or magnitude. No supporting analysis or approval memo could be located for either adjustment at the time of the review.

Compliance monitoring showed that sanctions list updates were being loaded manually and took effect two to four days after publication in 5 of the 12 weeks sampled. During those intervals, screening ran against outdated lists. No documented control was in place to confirm timely loading or to escalate delays.

The risk review concluded that sanctions list updates were being loaded manually, and in 5 of the 12 weeks sampled the load took place two to four days after the updated list became available. During those intervals, payments and customer records were screened against an outdated list. No compensating rescreen was evidenced for the affected periods.

Second-line testing found that the business continuity plans supporting five critical processes had not been updated or re-approved in more than two years. Because of this, recovery steps, contact details and dependencies documented in those plans may no longer reflect current operations. The gap was identified during the periodic review of continuity planning, and the affected process owners have been notified.

The risk review concluded that five processes designated as critical were operating under business continuity plans last updated more than two years ago. The plans had not been refreshed to reflect current staffing, recovery dependencies or contact details. As a result, recovery steps may no longer be workable if a disruption occurs.

Second-line testing found that the business continuity plans for five processes designated as critical had not been updated in more than two years. The stale plans may no longer match current recovery dependencies, staffing or system configurations. No evidence was provided that the plan owners had completed an interim review or attestation during that period.

The risk review concluded that the runoff rates applied to uninsured commercial deposits in the liquidity stress scenarios have not been revisited since 2021. These assumptions have carried forward into each subsequent stress cycle without any documented second-line challenge of their reasonableness against current deposit behavior.

The risk review concluded that duplicate item detection for check deposits was not applied to items received through remote deposit capture for a period of three months following a system upgrade. During that window, checks presented through the remote channel were not screened against previously deposited items, leaving the bank exposed to duplicate presentment and related check fraud losses that would otherwise have been flagged.

Second-line testing found that covenant compliance calculations were completed after the required due date for 11 of the 40 borrowers sampled during the review period. In addition, two covenant breaches identified within the sample had no documented waiver or approved exception on file, so the breaches remained unresolved and were not escalated to Credit Administration as required.

Independent risk testing found that loan review assigned lower risk grades to 9 of the 60 credits in the sample, but four of those downgrades had still not been booked to the loan records more than 60 days after the review. Until these grade changes are booked, the affected credits continue to be reported at their prior, more favorable ratings, so grade-dependent reporting and reserve inputs are stale for that period.

Independent risk testing found that loan review assigned lower risk grades to 9 of the 60 credits in the sample, but four of those downgrades remained unrecorded in the loan system of record for more than 60 days after the review conclusion. As a result, reported risk grades for these exposures did not reflect current credit quality during that period, which weakens the reliability of grade-driven reporting and reserve inputs.

Independent risk testing found that loan review downgraded 9 of the 60 credits sampled. Four of those downgrades had still not been booked to the risk rating of record more than 60 days after loan review made them, so reported risk grades overstated credit quality for that period.

Independent risk testing found that the loan review function downgraded 9 of the 60 credits selected for sample, but four of those downgrades remained unrecorded in the risk rating of record for more than 60 days after the review conclusion. During that period, the affected credits continued to carry their prior, more favorable grades in reserve, concentration and watch list reporting. Second line has not seen evidence of a control that tracks approved downgrades through to booking within a defined timeframe.

Compliance monitoring showed that complaints received at branches were entered into the complaint log an average of nine days after receipt, which delayed tracking and assignment for resolution. In the population reviewed, 31 complaints remained open beyond 15 days with no escalation to the Complaints Manager or other designated reviewer.

Second-line testing found that two incentive plans paid out on accounts that were later closed because the customer had not consented to opening them. Neither plan included a clawback or a deferral period tied to account validity, so employees kept the payments after the accounts were closed. The plan design also did not require any check of customer consent before incentive credit was granted.

Second-line testing found that 22 high-severity cyber threat detection alerts had been closed with no investigation notes recorded. Without documented analysis, there is no evidence that the alerts were triaged or that the closure rationale was reviewed before disposition. Information Security could not show whether the underlying activity was assessed as benign or escalated as appropriate.

The risk review concluded that 22 high-severity cyber threat detection alerts had been closed with no investigation notes recorded. Without that documentation, the review could not confirm that each alert was triaged, assessed for impact, or properly dispositioned before closure. Information Security has not shown that closure without supporting notes is restricted or subject to secondary review.

Compliance monitoring showed that 38 critical data elements were operating without an assigned owner and had no data quality rules defined against them. As a result, there is no accountable party responsible for the accuracy and completeness of these elements and no routine checks in place to detect errors before the data is used downstream.

Compliance monitoring showed that 38 critical data elements lacked both a designated owner and any defined quality rules, leaving no accountable party to validate accuracy or completeness. Because no rules exist, these elements receive no ongoing quality checks. Errors could therefore pass undetected into downstream reporting and risk processes.

Independent risk testing found that 38 critical data elements lacked both a designated owner and any defined data quality rules. Without ownership or rules in place, there is no assurance that these elements are monitored for completeness or accuracy, and no accountable party exists to remediate defects when they occur.

Second-line testing found that provisional credit was not posted within the required timeframe on 13 of the 50 consumer error claims sampled. The late credits were spread across the review period rather than clustered in a single month, which indicates the timeliness gap is not isolated to one processing backlog.

Second-line testing found that provisional credit was not posted to the customer's account within the required timeframe on 13 of the 50 consumer error claims sampled. In each exception the claim remained open past the provisional credit deadline without a documented reason for the delay, which indicates the current claim intake and tracking process is not reliably prompting timely credit.

Compliance monitoring showed that the weekly large depositor concentration report went unproduced for five consecutive weeks while the system conversion was underway. No alternate or manual report was prepared during that period, so concentration levels went unreviewed for the full five weeks.

Second-line testing found that margin calls on swap counterparty exposures went out one business day after they were due on 6 of the 25 dates sampled. During those delays the bank carried uncollateralized exposure above the agreed thresholds until the calls were issued and settled.

The risk review concluded that recovery testing for three critical services was performed in isolation, without exercising the upstream and downstream dependencies those services rely on in an actual outage. One of the three services did not restore within its stated recovery time objective during the exercise. As a result, the test results give limited assurance that the services could be recovered as designed under realistic conditions.

Second-line testing found that recovery exercises for three critical services were run in isolation, without their upstream and downstream dependencies in scope. As a result, the demonstrated recovery capability does not reflect a realistic outage. One of the three services also failed to meet its recovery objective during the exercise.

Independent risk testing found that the deposit beta assumptions used in interest rate risk modeling were last recalibrated 26 months ago, which leaves the current rate sensitivity outputs resting on aged pass-through estimates. Testing further noted that the quarterly back-testing results were not taken to ALCO in two quarters, so the committee did not receive evidence of model performance against actual deposit pricing behavior during those periods.

Second-line testing found that the automated fee tolerance checks were turned off for one loan product, so disclosed fees were never compared against tolerance limits before closing. Because of this gap, 19 loans exceeded the allowable thresholds and required restitution to borrowers.

The risk review concluded that automated fee tolerance checks had been turned off for one loan product, allowing disclosed fees to move beyond permitted tolerances without being flagged before closing. As a result, 19 loans were identified as requiring restitution to borrowers. No compensating manual review of fee changes was in place for that product while the checks were disabled.

The risk review concluded that fee tolerance checks had been turned off for a single loan product, so disclosed fees were not validated against tolerance limits before closing. As a result, 19 loans exceeded allowable fee variances and now require restitution to the affected borrowers.

Independent risk testing found that sixty adjustable-rate loans were not repriced on schedule, with each loan's rate reset occurring more than one month after the contractual reset date. Borrowers on these loans continued to be billed at the prior rate during the lag, and the exceptions were not identified by first-line payment processing controls before second-line review.

Second-line testing found that sixty adjustable-rate loans did not reprice on their scheduled reset date. In each case the rate change was posted more than one month late. As a result, borrower payments during the gap were calculated at the prior rate and not at the contractually required adjusted rate.

Compliance monitoring showed that four models remained in production use even though their scheduled validations were more than 12 months past due. No interim approval or documented exception was found that would support continued use of these models while validation was outstanding.

Compliance monitoring showed that four models remained in active production use although their scheduled validations were more than 12 months past due. No interim review or documented exception was on file to support continued reliance on these models while the validations remained outstanding.

The risk review concluded that two product changes were classified as minor and launched without review by the New Product Committee or completion of a risk assessment. The minor change designation was applied without documented criteria supporting it. As a result, neither change received the governance oversight required before launch.

Compliance monitoring showed that data loss prevention rules covering customer information were left in monitor-only mode for a four-month period, so matches were logged but no outbound transmissions were blocked. During that time 240 rule matches accumulated without being reviewed or dispositioned by anyone, and no assessment has yet been made of whether customer data left the bank.

Second-line testing found that nine clearing accounts carried reconciling items aged beyond 90 days, with the open balances totalling $1.2 million. The aged items had not been resolved or escalated within the expected timeframe.

Second-line testing found that nine clearing accounts were carrying reconciling items aged beyond 90 days, with the combined balance of those stale items reaching $1.2 million at the review date. Because financial statement due dates on construction loans funded in draws are tracked through a manual tickler, borrower financial covenant breaches may go undetected in the period between annual reviews. As a result, credit deterioration may be recognized too late for the unit to restructure, tighten draw conditions, or take other protective action before further funds are advanced.

Borrower financial statements on construction loans funded in draws are frequently spread months after they fall due, because receipt is tracked only through a manual tickler, leaving financial covenant breaches unnoticed by the unit in the interval between annual reviews. As a result, credit deterioration may be recognized too late for the unit to restructure, tighten draw conditions, or take other protective action before any further funds are advanced.

Because financial statement due dates for booked business credits are tracked through a manual tickler, missed or late borrower submissions may not be followed up, and financial covenant breaches can go undetected in the interval between annual reviews. As a result, credit deterioration may be recognized too late for the bank to restructure terms, require additional collateral, or take other protective action.

Because financial statement due dates for financed machinery and vehicles borrowers are tracked through a manual tickler, missed or late submissions may go unflagged and financial covenant breaches may not be identified between annual reviews. Credit deterioration could then be recognized too late to act, limiting options to restructure, require additional collateral or reduce exposure before losses emerge.

Because financial statement due dates for owner-operated company loans are tracked through a manual tickler process, borrower statements may be spread months after they are due, so covenant breaches go unidentified and credit deterioration is recognized too late for the unit to take protective action.

Relationship managers who assign their own credit grades may favor optimistic assessments. As a result, ratings on income-producing property loans may stay unchanged even as debt service cash flow declines and payments are missed. Stale grades of this kind could leave the allowance understated and delay referral of deteriorating credits to workout.

Because relationship managers assign the grades on booked business credits and tend to view their own borrowers optimistically, risk ratings may not be downgraded promptly when borrower financial performance deteriorates during ongoing oversight. That could leave the credit loss reserve understated and delay transfer of weakening loans to workout until recovery options have narrowed.

Credit grades on booked business credits are set by the relationship managers who own those borrowers and often stay unchanged through declining cash flow and missed payments, so risk ratings may not be downgraded when borrower performance weakens during ongoing oversight. This could leave the credit loss reserve understated and delay the transfer of weakening loans to workout until recovery options have narrowed.

Because relationship managers tend to assign optimistic grades to their own borrowers, risk ratings may not be downgraded promptly when borrower performance deteriorates, and independent credit quality checks may fail to catch and correct those stale grades. As a result, reserves could be understated and workout action on weakening credits could start later than it should.

Because relationship managers assign risk grades to mid-sized corporate borrowers and may view their own relationships with optimism bias, credit grades may remain unchanged even as borrower cash flow declines and payments are missed. The result could be understated reserves and workout action that begins too late to protect the bank's position.

Owing to optimism bias in the credit grades that relationship managers assign and maintain, ratings on loans to high-net-worth clients may remain static even as borrower cash flow deteriorates and scheduled payments are missed. This could result in understated loss reserves and delayed referral of weakening credits for workout action.

Because the bank has no single intake channel for complaints, verbal complaints raised by customers in branches about cardholder chargebacks may never be logged in the complaint system. Those complaints could then go unresolved, leaving customer harm unaddressed and creating UDAAP exposure.

Because there is no single intake channel for complaints in phone-based customer service, verbal complaints raised with branch staff may never be logged in the complaint system. These complaints can then go untracked and unresolved, leaving customer harm unaddressed and exposing the bank to UDAAP risk.

Because the bank has no single intake channel for customer complaints, complaints received in branches may not be logged or resolved on time as client dissatisfaction items, which could leave customer harm unaddressed and expose the bank to UDAAP risk.

Because the complaint categories used for cardholder chargebacks are defined too broadly, recurring complaint themes may go without root cause analysis. Underlying issues could then persist unaddressed, exposing customers to repeat harm and the bank to reputational damage.

Because complaint data for cardholder chargebacks is reported only as counts, with no step to identify systemic issues, recurring complaint themes in cardholder chargebacks are not analyzed for root causes. Underlying issues could therefore persist unaddressed, exposing customers to repeat harm and the bank to reputational damage.

Because complaint categories used in retail regulation testing are defined too broadly, recurring complaint themes may go without root cause analysis, so the same underlying issues are not identified or corrected. This could allow repeat customer harm and expose the bank to reputational damage.

Collector staffing has not kept pace with growth in delinquency, so past-due and charged-off accounts may not be worked within the required timeframes as queues build and contact attempts slip. This could result in higher charge-offs and in borrowers falling back into delinquency after their accounts are cured.

Collector headcount in personal term loans has not kept pace with rising delinquency, and work queues are not prioritized by risk or days past due, so past-due accounts may roll into later aging buckets without any contact from a collector. This could drive higher charge-offs and repeat delinquency among borrowers who cure only briefly before falling behind again.

Because collector staffing has not kept pace with growth in delinquencies across the revolving retail lending portfolio, delinquent accounts may not be worked within required timeframes. This could lead to higher charge-offs and repeat delinquency among borrowers who are not contacted promptly.

Because collector staffing has not kept pace with rising delinquency in dealer-originated vehicle contracts, delinquent accounts may go unworked within required timeframes, leading to higher charge-offs and a greater incidence of repeat delinquency across the portfolio.

Because collector staffing has not kept pace with growth in delinquency across escrow and loss mitigation on home loans, work queues are left unprioritized and past-due accounts can roll into later aging buckets with no borrower contact attempted. This could drive higher charge-offs and a greater rate of repeat delinquency among accounts that were previously cured.

Collector staffing in escrow and loss mitigation on home loans has fallen behind the growth in delinquency, so delinquent accounts are not being worked within required timeframes and the unit is exposed when unprioritized queues let past-due accounts age into later buckets without any attempt at borrower contact. This could drive higher charge-offs and a greater rate of repeat delinquency among accounts that had previously cured.

Because collection queues for owner-operated company loans are not prioritized and collector staffing has not kept pace with delinquency growth, past-due accounts may age without any borrower contact. The bank could then see higher charge-offs and repeat delinquency in the portfolio.

Because incentive plans for in-person teller and banker activity are designed and owned solely by the business lines without independent input, plans may reward account openings and product sales volume with no adjustment for risk or customer outcomes. This could drive inappropriate sales to customers and give rise to conduct issues at the branch level.

Because incentive plan design for client securities trading is owned solely by the business lines, with no requirement to claw back payouts when sales are later reversed, staff may be rewarded for trades that are subsequently unwound or cancelled. Representatives could then pursue volume at the expense of suitability, producing inappropriate sales and conduct issues that lead to client harm, remediation costs, regulatory criticism and reputational damage.

Because variable pay plans are designed and owned solely by the business lines, incentives may reward sales volume without regard to risk or customer outcomes. This could lead to inappropriate sales practices and other conduct issues, resulting in customer harm, remediation costs, regulatory criticism and reputational damage to the bank.

Incentive plan design is owned solely by the business lines, with no independent review of how payouts behave after a sale is reversed, so employee pay runs may release incentive payouts that are never clawed back when the underlying sales are later unwound. This could reward volume over suitability and encourage inappropriate sales and related conduct issues.

Concentration reporting is built on funded balances only and does not pick up commitments, so the unfunded portion of draw-based construction loans to builders is left out of reported commercial real estate concentration. As a result, true exposure may be understated and limits breached without detection, which could lead to outsized losses if property values decline.

Because concentration reporting omits unfunded commitments, income-producing property loan exposure may grow beyond Board concentration limits without triggering escalation, leaving the bank with outsized credit losses if property values and cash flows decline in a downturn.

Alert volumes routinely exceed analyst capacity in round-the-clock threat monitoring, so malicious network activity may sit untriaged in the queue and go undetected or uncontained for an extended period. That delay could allow data theft and disruption of customer-facing and internal services before Information Security is able to respond.

Because alert volumes in hosted infrastructure routinely exceed analyst capacity, security alerts may be closed without investigation during high-volume periods, allowing an intrusion to go undetected. This could result in theft of bank data and disruption of services that depend on the hosted environment.

Because security alert volumes for customer self-service channels exceed what available analysts can triage, malicious activity on the network may go undetected or may not be contained quickly. This could allow theft of customer data and disrupt service across those channels.

Because alert volumes in the same-day outgoing payments environment can exceed analyst capacity during high-volume periods, security alerts may be closed without investigation, allowing cyber intrusions to go undetected and resulting in data theft and disruption to payment services.

Because data quality checks over the critical data elements feeding expected loss reserving run only at month end, incomplete or inaccurate inputs can flow into reserve models and supporting reports without timely detection. Reserve estimates and reported results may then be misstated, and the errors may not be found until after figures have been relied upon for close and management review.

Because data quality checks on the critical data elements behind internal charges for funding run only at month end, incomplete or inaccurate inputs can flow into the reports and models that rely on them without being detected during the period. Misstated reports and model results could then be used to set and evaluate funding charges, with errors found only after the period has closed and decisions have already been made.

Because data quality checks on critical data elements run only at month end, errors and gaps in the inputs that feed supervisory filings and models can go undetected through most of the reporting cycle. Incomplete or inaccurate data may then flow into regulatory reports and model outputs, causing misstated filings, unreliable model results, and possible supervisory criticism or rework under tight submission deadlines.

Because error claims and claim deadlines raised through in-person teller and banker activity are tracked manually, staff may fail to meet error resolution timelines or apply fund availability rules correctly. This could result in regulatory findings and harm to customers.

Because Deposit Operations tracks claim deadlines manually, consumer error claims involving inactive balances owed to states may not be resolved within regulatory timeframes. This could lead to regulatory findings and customer harm, including delayed restoration of funds to affected account holders.

Because claim deadlines for electronic error disputes submitted through customer self-service channels are tracked manually, error claim timelines and fund availability requirements may not be met consistently for claims and deposits originating in those channels. This could result in regulatory findings and customer harm, such as delayed provisional credit or improperly held funds.

Because large commercial operating balances in business client cash management have grown, the unit's uninsured deposits are concentrated in a small number of clients, and a few of those large depositors could pull their balances faster than the bank can replace the funding. The result would likely be a sudden funding gap that Treasury would need to cover at short notice, potentially at a higher cost and with added strain on liquidity metrics reported to ALCO.

Because collateral requirements for swap counterparties supporting cross-currency client payments are calculated manually outside the treasury system, exposure to those counterparties may exceed approved limits without collateral calls being made. If an under-collateralized counterparty then defaults, the bank could incur losses on the uncovered portion of the exposure.

Because collateral requirements on the swaps hedging the balance sheet are calculated manually outside the treasury system, exposure to swap counterparties may exceed approved limits without collateral being called. If a counterparty defaults while that exposure is uncollateralized, the bank could incur losses on replacing the hedge and lose protection on the hedged balance sheet positions.

Because disaster recovery tests for phone-based customer service are scoped to single applications and skip critical dependencies, recovery gaps may go undetected until a real disruption. This could lead to prolonged outages of customer-facing services and leave customers unable to reach the bank by phone for extended periods.

Because disaster recovery testing for hosted infrastructure is scoped to individual applications and leaves out the critical shared dependencies those applications rely on, the bank may be unable to restore customer-facing services within required recovery times during an actual outage. Customers could lose access to services for an extended period, causing financial loss, regulatory criticism and reputational damage.

Because disaster recovery testing in production technology operations is scoped to single applications, critical dependencies between systems go unexercised, so recovery steps may fail or run long in a real event. Critical systems could then not be restored within required timeframes, leading to prolonged outages of customer-facing services.

Disaster recovery tests in production technology operations skip critical dependencies because each exercise is scoped to a single application, so the recovery sequence across interconnected systems is never proven against recovery time objectives and steps may fail or take longer than planned during an actual event. Critical systems could then fail to be restored within required timeframes, leading to prolonged outages of customer-facing services.

Because recovery testing for instant account-to-account transfers has been scoped to individual applications rather than the end-to-end processing chain, the critical applications supporting the service may not be restorable within their recovery time objectives during a disruption. This could result in prolonged outages of customer-facing transfer services.

Because loan officers hold broad pricing discretion over revolving retail lending decisions, they may grant pricing exceptions without recording a documented reason. This could produce unexplained pricing disparities across borrowers, resulting in customer harm and exposure to regulatory action for fair lending violations.

Because loan officers have broad pricing discretion, they may grant pricing exceptions without documenting the reasons, which could produce unjustified pricing disparities in equitable credit pricing and access. This could result in harm to customers and regulatory action against the bank.

Because loan officers have broad discretion to grant pricing exceptions on second-lien credit lines secured by residences, exception pricing may produce rate and fee disparities across protected groups, exposing the bank to regulatory action and harm to affected borrowers.

Because loan officers hold broad discretion over pricing on dealer-originated vehicle contracts, they may grant pricing exceptions without recording a reason, which leaves similarly situated borrowers on unequal terms that the bank cannot explain or defend. This could lead to customer harm through unjustified rate disparities and expose the bank to fair lending scrutiny and regulatory action.

Because trust officer caseloads in decedent asset administration exceed policy limits, officers may administer trust and estate accounts outside the terms of the governing documents, for example by distributing to beneficiaries before required conditions are met or by missing directed asset dispositions. This exposes the unit to surcharge claims from beneficiaries and to litigation.

Because trust officer caseloads run above the levels set in policy, trust and estate accounts in individual fiduciary relationships may be administered in ways that depart from their governing documents, such as missed distribution terms or investment restrictions. The unit would then face beneficiary surcharge claims and litigation, along with the associated remediation cost and reputational harm.

Because payment outflows are concentrated in the afternoon, the bank's intraday funding buffer may prove insufficient to fund outflows at peak times during the day. This could leave payments failed or delayed and expose the bank to overdraft fees.

Because outgoing same-day payment volume is concentrated in the afternoon, intraday overdraft positions in the Federal Reserve account may not be monitored in real time as same-day outgoing payments are released. Payments could then be released against insufficient funds, resulting in failed or delayed settlement and the bank incurring overdraft fees.

Due to reliance on manual compilation of the interest rate risk limit report for swaps hedging the balance sheet, limit breaches under rate shock scenarios may be detected late and never escalated to the Board. That could leave the bank carrying unmanaged exposure to rising rates.

Because the interest rate limit report for the bond holdings kept for liquidity is compiled manually, breaches of limits under rate shock scenarios may be identified late and never reported to the Board. This could leave the bank with unmanaged exposure to rising rates, with losses in the liquidity portfolio building before management or the Board can respond.

Because the interest rate limit report is compiled manually, an economic value of equity sensitivity that exceeds Board limits under rising rate scenarios may go undetected and unescalated. The bank could then carry unmanaged balance sheet rate exposure, with resulting losses to economic value and breaches of Board-approved risk appetite.

Because deposit assumptions used in internal charges for funding are not put through an annual assumption review and have become outdated, the ALM model may misstate earnings sensitivity, which could lead Treasury and ALCO to base hedging decisions on misleading rate sensitivity results.

Because the annual assumption review has not been performed, deposit repricing betas feeding the earnings-at-risk measure for balance sheet rate exposure may still reflect conditions from before the recent rate movements. As a result, the unit's reported rate sensitivity could be misleading, leading Treasury and ALCO to base hedging decisions on an inaccurate view of NII exposure.

Because fees are keyed manually into personal term loan documents, closing disclosures may be issued inside the required waiting period, exposing the unit to customer restitution and regulatory penalties.

Because fees for first-lien home purchase and refinance loans are keyed into loan documents by hand, required consumer disclosures may go out late or with errors. This could lead to borrower restitution and regulatory penalties.

Because fees are keyed manually into loan documents for revolving retail lending decisions, closing disclosures may be inaccurate and may be delivered to borrowers inside the required waiting period. This could expose the bank to customer restitution and regulatory penalties.

Because fees on second-lien credit lines secured by residences are keyed manually into the loan documents, closing disclosures may be issued inside the required waiting period with inaccurate figures. The bank could then owe borrowers restitution and face regulatory penalties.

Because fees on dealer-originated vehicle contracts are keyed manually into the loan documents, closing disclosures may be inaccurate or delivered to borrowers inside the required waiting period, which could expose the bank to customer restitution and regulatory penalties.

Because fees are keyed manually into home loan documents, required consumer disclosures covering escrow and loss mitigation may be issued late or contain errors, which could expose the bank to restitution to affected borrowers and to regulatory penalties.

Because loan terms on the financed machinery and vehicle portfolio are maintained manually after boarding, adjustable-rate loans may fail to reprice on their scheduled dates, causing incorrect payment amounts that harm customers and require refunds.

Because loan terms are maintained manually once a loan has been boarded, rate change dates and index or margin values may be keyed incorrectly or left unchanged in credit setup and repayment posting, so adjustable-rate loans can fail to reprice when scheduled. This can lead to borrowers being billed incorrect payment amounts, misapplied repayments, customer harm, and refunds or account remediation once the errors are found.

Because loan terms on government-guaranteed company loans are maintained manually after boarding, adjustable-rate loans in this portfolio may not reprice on their scheduled dates, causing incorrect payment and escrow amounts. Borrowers could be harmed and the unit would have to issue refunds.

Because business lines build spreadsheet tools outside the model policy, tools that function as models in expected loss reserving are never recorded in the model inventory and are used without independent validation. Reserve decisions may then rest on flawed model output, which could misstate expected loss reserves.

Because business lines build spreadsheet tools outside the model policy, tools that function as models in the enterprise AML program may go unrecorded in the model inventory and so escape validation. Decisions in the AML program could then rest on flawed output that nobody has independently tested, leaving the bank exposed to monitoring gaps and unreliable risk conclusions.

Because business lines build spreadsheet tools outside the model policy, tools that behave like models in the enterprise AML program are missing from the model inventory, and some begin driving decisions before independent validation is complete. Decisions in the AML program could then rest on flawed output that no one has independently tested, leaving the bank exposed to monitoring gaps and unreliable risk conclusions.

Because business lines build spreadsheet tools outside the model policy, tools that function as models in suspicious card activity handling may be left out of the model inventory and never validated. Decisions on flagged card activity could then rest on flawed model output.

Because business lines build spreadsheet tools outside the model policy, tools that function as models for internal charges for funding are not captured in the model inventory and so are never validated. Pricing, profitability and balance sheet decisions may then rest on flawed output that no one has independently reviewed.

Because business lines build quantitative tools outside the model policy, models may be used to drive decisions before independent validation is complete, which weakens oversight of quantitative tools. As a result, the unit could make lending, pricing or reporting decisions based on flawed model output without timely detection.

Because business lines build spreadsheet tools outside the model policy, tools that function as models for balance sheet interest rate exposure are not captured in the model inventory and so are never validated. Rate exposure decisions may then rely on flawed or unchallenged model output, leading to misstated risk positions and poorly informed management actions.

Because the criteria defining what counts as a new product remain unclear, changes to the corporate purchasing card offering may be classified as minor so that they bypass New Product Committee review. As a result, features could launch without a risk assessment, leaving compliance and operational exposures unidentified and unmanaged.

Because the criteria for what counts as a new product are unclear, product launches and changes to existing offerings may go live before compliance and operational risk reviews are complete, leaving the bank exposed to compliance and operational risks that have not been identified, assessed or brought under management.

Because the criteria for what counts as a new product are unclear, changes to customer self-service channels may be labelled minor so they bypass the New Product Committee and launch without a formal risk assessment. Compliance and operational exposures could then go unidentified and unmanaged until after customers are already using the changed features.

Because business sponsors negotiate and sign contracts with fintech partners before third-party risk management is engaged, critical vendors may be onboarded for product launches and offering changes before their security and financial reviews are complete. Customers could then be exposed to an unvetted partner's control weaknesses, causing consumer harm and regulatory criticism that examiners and the public would attribute to the bank rather than the vendor.

Business sponsors frequently negotiate and finalize contract terms with outsourced service providers before third-party risk management has been brought in. This creates a risk that critical vendors, including fintech partners, are onboarded and begin servicing customers before their security and financial reviews are complete, which could result in consumer harm and regulatory criticism attributed to the bank.

Because data loss prevention rules supporting client securities trading remain in monitor-only mode and do not block outbound transmissions, customer personal information may be shared with or accessed by parties beyond what customers consented to. This could result in privacy breaches requiring customer notification, along with the associated notification costs and reputational harm to the bank.

Because data loss prevention rules for phone-based customer service remain in monitor-only mode, outbound email carrying customer files is not blocked. Customer files could therefore be sent outside the bank without detection, exposing customers to privacy breaches and the bank to notification costs.

Because data loss prevention rules for enterprise information stewardship operate in monitor-only mode and do not block outbound transmissions, customer files may be sent outside the bank by email without being detected or stopped. This could result in privacy breaches affecting customers and in the bank incurring notification costs along with related remediation effort.

Because data loss prevention rules covering customer self-service channels run in monitor-only mode and do not block outbound transfers, personal information may be shared with or accessed by parties beyond what customers consented to. Such a disclosure would expose the bank to privacy breaches, customer notification costs, and related remediation effort and reputational harm.

Because data loss prevention rules on outbound email are set to monitor-only mode and do not block transmissions, customer files tied to new advisory relationships could be emailed outside the bank without being detected or stopped. Such an unauthorized disclosure would expose the bank to a privacy breach and the resulting customer notification costs.

Because reconciliation ownership for payment suspense accounts is split between operations and finance, with neither function clearly accountable for researching and clearing aged items, entries from batch electronic debits and credits may remain unresolved past expected clearing timeframes. This could result in misstated balances and losses that go undetected until well after the original posting.

Because reconciliation ownership for cardholder chargeback suspense accounts is split between operations and finance, aged items may not be researched or cleared in a timely manner. This could lead to misstated balances and to losses going undetected until they are written off.

Because ownership of payment suspense reconciliations is split between operations and finance, balances in month-end accounting can age beyond 30 days without being escalated to anyone accountable for clearing them. Items can then sit unresolved through the close, which may result in misstated balances and in losses that go undetected until they are written off or surfaced at a later review.

Because reconciliation ownership for supplier invoice settlement is spread across several teams, reconciling items in the clearing accounts may age past policy limits without being escalated. This could leave balances misstated and allow errors to go undetected.

Reconciliation ownership for the clearing accounts that hold inactive balances owed to states is divided among several teams with no single accountable owner, so reconciling items may age beyond policy limits without being escalated. These balances could then be misstated, and errors could go undetected until escheatment reporting or a later review.

Because reconciliation ownership for the employer-sponsored savings contributions clearing accounts is split across multiple teams with no single accountable owner, reconciling items may age beyond policy limits without being escalated. Balances could then be misstated and errors could go undetected.

Because month-end accounting relies heavily on manual adjustments posted outside the reporting system, material errors may be carried into call reports and other regulatory filings, which could require resubmission of the affected filings and expose the bank to supervisory criticism.

Because manual adjustments to the source feeds for supervisory filings are made outside the reporting system, reported figures may not be reconciled to the ledger before submission. Unreconciled figures could force resubmission of filings and draw supervisory criticism of the bank's reporting controls.

Where regulatory report figures in the source feeds for supervisory filings are changed through manual adjustments made outside the reporting system, call reports and other regulatory filings may be submitted with material errors because those figures were never reconciled to the ledger before submission. Unreconciled figures could force resubmission of filings and draw supervisory criticism of the bank's regulatory reporting controls.

Because preparers post manual adjustments outside the reporting system, call reports and other regulatory filings may be submitted with material errors, leading to required resubmissions and supervisory criticism of the bank's reporting controls.

Reliance on a single external pricing source for thinly traded bonds in client securities trading may allow vendor prices to be accepted without independent challenge or price verification, resulting in misstated fair values and capital.

Reliance on one external pricing source, with no independent price verification or tolerance checks for thinly traded bonds in the securities portfolio held for liquidity, may allow vendor-supplied prices to be accepted month after month without challenge. Stale or inaccurate marks could then misstate the fair values reported for these holdings and, in turn, the bank's capital position.

Because securities in the bond holdings kept for liquidity are carried at prices from a single external pricing source, with no independent price verification and no tolerance checks, vendor prices for thinly traded bonds may be accepted without challenge in each month-end valuation cycle. Stale or inaccurate marks could then misstate the reported fair values for these holdings and, in turn, the bank's capital position.

Because pricing for securities held in discretionary client investment accounts relies on a single source without independent verification, positions may be carried at inaccurate prices, resulting in misstated fair values and a corresponding misstatement of capital.

Because income and franchise tax obligations are governed by complex rules and are prepared by a small team with limited capacity for independent review, there is a risk that the tax accounts are not reconciled to the returns as actually filed. This could result in penalties and a restatement of earnings.

Because exception trades in discretionary client investment accounts are still entered into the order system by hand, keying errors may go undetected. When they are caught, correction can come late and the affected client may not be told. The bank is then exposed to client losses that it must reimburse, together with the associated complaint and conduct risk.

Because exceptions to employer-sponsored savings contributions are keyed through manual order entry, client trades and contributions may post late or to the wrong account, exposing the bank to client losses and the cost of reimbursing affected participants.

Because high volumes of credit setup and repayment posting exceptions are worked by hand, manual adjustments to customer accounts may be keyed and released without maker-checker review. Incorrect balances, payment allocations or loan terms could then go undetected, leading to customer harm and operational losses from remediation and write-offs.

Because high volumes of escrow and loss mitigation exceptions on home loans are worked by hand, manual adjustments to customer accounts may be posted without maker-checker review. Incorrect balances, payments, or escrow amounts could then go undetected, causing customer harm and operational losses for the unit.

Because teller and banker sales goals are tied to product counts, employees in branch and other in-person channels may be pressured to open accounts or enroll customers in products they did not request or authorize. This could cause customer harm, require remediation and refunds, and expose the bank to regulatory enforcement action and reputational damage.

Where teller and banker sales goals are measured on product counts, staff in branches and other in-person channels may feel pressure to push unwanted products, leading to accounts being opened or products added for customers who neither requested nor authorized them. This could result in customer harm, require remediation and refunds, and expose the bank to regulatory enforcement action and reputational damage.

Incentive goals that reward employees on product counts may push staff to open or approve revolving retail credit accounts that customers did not request or consent to. This could result in customer harm, remediation costs and regulatory enforcement action against the bank.

Because variable pay plans set employee sales goals driven primarily by product counts, staff may be pressured to sell products customers do not want, including opening accounts without customer consent. This could cause customer harm and expose the bank to enforcement action.

Sales goals and incentives tied to product counts may pressure staff to open accounts or add products and services through customer self-service channels without the customer's request or informed consent. Such unauthorized activity could cause financial and reputational harm to affected customers and expose the bank to regulatory enforcement action, restitution, and penalties.

Because employees face sales goals and incentives tied to product counts that encourage unwanted product sales, there is a risk that accounts, products or services are opened or added through customer self-service channels for customers who did not request them or give informed consent. Such unauthorized activity could cause financial and reputational harm to affected customers and could expose the bank to regulatory enforcement action, restitution, and penalties.

Because approvers can manually override controls in the origination workflow, loans funded in draws during building projects may be approved for amounts above the approver's delegated lending authority. Because approvers can manually override controls in the origination workflow, income-producing property loans may be approved above the approver's delegated lending authority, which would create credit exposure the bank never sanctioned at the right approval level. Because manual overrides are permitted in the origination workflow, commercial credits for financed machinery and vehicles may close above the house limit without the required second signature, resulting in unapproved credit exposure and higher loss severity if these borrowers default.

Because the origination workflow allows manual overrides, loans to mid-sized corporate borrowers may be approved above the approver's delegated lending authority. This could create credit exposure that was never properly sanctioned and could increase loss severity if those borrowers default.

Because manual overrides in the origination workflow allow files to advance without enforced approval checks, commercial credits in the owner-operated company loan portfolio may close without the second signature required for exposures above the house limit. Because the origination workflow allows manual overrides, commercial credits shared with other lenders may close above the house limit without the required second signature. This could leave the bank with credit exposure that was never properly approved and with greater loss severity if those participations deteriorate.

Because appraisal ordering for new business credit requests is handled by the loan officer, collateral values relied on in underwriting may be stale or lack support from an independent appraisal. Because the loan officer originating the credit is also the person who orders the appraisal, collateral values relied on in underwriting first-lien home purchase and refinance loans may be stale or lack support from an independent appraisal. Valuations may then overstate the property securing the loan, leaving loss given default understated in credit decisions, pricing and reserve estimates.

Because appraisal ordering for income-producing property loans is handled by the originating loan officer, collateral values relied on in underwriting may be stale or lack the support of an independent appraisal. Loss given default would then be understated and credit exposure on the affected loans misjudged at origination.

Because loan officers order appraisals directly for second-lien home equity lines of credit, appraisals may be accepted without any review of the appraiser's independence or the comparable sales relied upon.
